15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.why_it_exists: Unit tests with mocks verify that code uses collaborators correctly assuming the collaborators work as expected. Integration tests verify that assumption: the real database has different behaviour than a mock (SQL constraints, transaction semantics, index performance). A common failure mode: unit tests pass with mocks; integration tests fail because the ORM generates incorrect SQL, or a database trigger fires unexpectedly, or message serialization doesn't round-trip correctly.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.use_when: Write integration tests for: API endpoints (full request/response cycle), repository layer (SQL queries against real database), message consumers (Kafka/RabbitMQ consumers with real brokers via TestContainers), authentication/authorization flows, and any integration with external services (mocked at the HTTP boundary with WireMock, not the service class level).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.avoid_when: Avoid integration tests for: pure business logic (unit tests are faster and more precise), tests that would require production credentials (mock the external API at the HTTP layer), and tests that are too slow to run in CI (> 5 minutes for the full suite). Integration tests are slow — run the critical path integration tests in CI, full integration suite in nightly builds.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.what_goes_wrong:
- Shared state between tests: tests running against the same database instance leave data that pollutes subsequent tests. Fix: wrap each test in a transaction that's rolled back after the test, or use a unique schema per test, or recreate the container per test (expensive but clean). `IAsyncLifetime` + `IClassFixture` in xUnit control setup/teardown scope.
- TestContainers cold start: Docker image pull + container start can take 30-60 seconds the first time. Use `ClassFixture` to share one container across all tests in a class, not per-test container startup.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.real_example: GitHub's CI for a .NET microservice: unit tests run in <30 seconds (10,000 tests). Integration tests run in 4 minutes (300 tests): 50 API tests via `WebApplicationFactory` + PostgreSQL TestContainer, 100 repository tests against real Postgres, 150 message consumer tests against real RabbitMQ (TestContainers). A bug where the EF Core migration missed an index was caught only by integration tests — unit tests passed because the mock returned data instantly regardless of indexes.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.what_it_is: System testing (also called end-to-end testing or E2E testing) verifies the complete system from the user's perspective — simulating real user workflows across all layers (UI → API → service → database). Tools: Playwright or Cypress for browser-based E2E tests (click buttons, fill forms, navigate pages), Postman/Newman for API-level E2E, Selenium for legacy browser automation. System tests check that all system components work together to deliver business value: 'a user can register, log in, add items to cart, checkout, receive a confirmation email, and see the order in their account.'
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.why_it_exists: Integration tests verify individual component connections; system tests verify the business workflow as a whole. An integration test may pass for each individual service while a workflow fails because of timing issues, session management problems, or third-party service failures that only manifest when all layers are running simultaneously. System tests are the final safety net before production.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.use_when: Write system tests for: critical business workflows (user registration → first purchase, onboarding flow, payment processing), regressions of critical bugs, and smoke tests for production deployments. Target 10-20% of test coverage in system tests (the 'happy path' and top error scenarios). System tests are the most expensive — run them on every PR for critical paths, full suite in staging before production deploy.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.avoid_when: Avoid system testing for: edge cases and error handling (integration/unit tests are more efficient), performance testing (use dedicated load testing tools like k6/Gatling), and testing every feature variant (test only the primary user journey, not every combination). Don't replace integration tests with system tests — system tests are too slow and fragile for comprehensive coverage.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.what_goes_wrong:
- Flakiness: E2E tests fail intermittently due to timing issues (`await page.click()` before the button is clickable, race conditions, slow CI machines). Fix: use Playwright's `waitFor` assertions (`await expect(element).toBeVisible()`) instead of arbitrary `sleep()` calls. Use `page.waitForURL()`, `page.waitForResponse()` for async operations.
- Test data pollution: E2E tests create real orders, users, and payments in the test environment. Without cleanup, data accumulates and tests interfere with each other. Fix: use unique test-run identifiers (prefix email with `test-{uuid}@`), always clean up created data in `afterEach`, or use dedicated test databases that are reset between CI runs.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.real_example: Shopify's E2E test suite runs checkout workflows on a staging environment against a real Stripe test API. The test creates a product, adds to cart, checks out with Stripe test card `4242424242424242`, verifies the order status, and checks that the merchant receives a payout notification. This catches integration failures between Shopify's checkout code and Stripe's API that unit/integration tests miss (e.g., a Stripe API version change that breaks 3DS authentication flows).

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.what_it_is: Acceptance testing verifies that the system satisfies business requirements and is acceptable for delivery to the customer. **User Acceptance Testing (UAT)**: business stakeholders/end users manually test the system against acceptance criteria using real-world scenarios. **Automated acceptance tests**: executable specifications (Cucumber/Gherkin, SpecFlow) that business people can read and developers execute: `Given I am a premium customer, When I apply discount code SAVE20, Then my cart total should decrease by 20%.` The distinction from system testing: acceptance testing asks 'does it solve the business problem?' not just 'does it work technically?'
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.why_it_exists: Technical testing (unit, integration, system) verifies the system works as specified. Acceptance testing verifies the specification itself was correct — that what was built is what the business needed. Teams can build technically correct software that fails UAT because the requirements were misunderstood, the UI workflow doesn't match how users actually work, or business rules were captured incorrectly. UAT is the final gate: production deployment only after business sign-off.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.how_it_works:
```gherkin
# Gherkin (Cucumber/SpecFlow) — readable by business stakeholders

Feature: Discount Code Application
  As a customer with a discount code
  I want to apply the code to my cart
  So that I receive the advertised discount

  Scenario: Valid 20% discount code applied to eligible cart
    Given I am logged in as a premium customer
    And my cart contains:
      | Product    | Price  | Qty |
      | Widget Pro | £50.00 | 2   |
    And the cart total is £100.00
    When I enter discount code "SAVE20"
    And I click "Apply discount"
    Then the cart total should be £80.00
    And I should see the message "20% discount applied"

  Scenario: Expired discount code rejected
    Given I am logged in as any customer
    When I enter discount code "EXPIRED10"
    And I click "Apply discount"
    Then I should see the error "This discount code has expired"
    And the cart total should be unchanged

  Scenario: Discount code not applicable to sale items
    Given my cart contains only sale items
    When I enter discount code "SAVE20"
    Then I should see "Discount codes cannot be applied to sale items"
```

```csharp
// SpecFlow step definitions (C#)
[Given(@"my cart contains:")] 
public void GivenMyCartContains(Table productTable) {
    var items = productTable.CreateSet<CartItem>();
    foreach (var item in items)
        _cartService.AddItem(item.Product, item.Qty);
}

[When(@"I enter discount code \""(.*)\""")]
public void WhenIEnterDiscountCode(string code) =>
    _discountCode = code;

[Then(@"the cart total should be £(.*)")] 
public void ThenCartTotalShouldBe(decimal expected) =>
    Assert.Equal(expected, _cartService.GetTotal(_discountCode));
```
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.use_when: Use formal UAT before every production release in: enterprise software (complex business rules, regulatory requirements), customer-facing applications with user journeys that can only be evaluated by real users, and any release with significant new functionality. Use automated acceptance tests (SpecFlow/Cucumber) for regression of accepted scenarios — run them in CI so UAT sign-off of scenarios is permanent.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.avoid_when: Avoid manual UAT for: pure backend services (no user-facing UI), minor bug fixes where the acceptance criteria is clear and unchanged, and internal developer tools. Don't use UAT as a substitute for integration/system testing — UAT catches business requirement gaps, not technical integration issues.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.what_goes_wrong:
- UAT too late: UAT scheduled for week 11 of a 12-week project reveals that a key workflow doesn't match how users actually work. Rework is possible but expensive. Fix: involve users in every sprint review — treat sprint demos as continuous mini-UAT so large surprises don't accumulate to the final UAT gate.
- Business stakeholders don't participate: 'UAT' conducted by QA engineers who test against requirements documents, not by actual end users. This misses usability issues and workflow mismatches that only domain experts notice. Real UAT requires real domain experts (nurses testing patient record software, accountants testing financial software) in a UAT environment with production-like data.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Software Testi.real_example: HMRC (UK tax authority) releases a new VAT filing portal: 4 weeks of UAT with 50 actual VAT-registered business owners from different sectors (retail, manufacturing, hospitality). They use the portal with their real VAT return data from the previous quarter. UAT catches: accountants couldn't figure out how to split import VAT from domestic VAT (a workflow issue), the help text was insufficient for partial exemption calculations, and the submission confirmation email was going to spam. All fixed before public launch. Without real users in UAT, these would have been discovered by 3 million VAT filers on launch day.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_it_is: Test-Driven Development (TDD) is a development process where you write the test before the implementation. The cycle: **Red** — write a failing test that describes the behaviour you want (it fails because the code doesn't exist yet). **Green** — write the minimum code needed to make the test pass (doesn't have to be clean). **Refactor** — clean up the code while keeping the tests green. The test suite is the specification; production code is written to satisfy the specification. Kent Beck introduced TDD as a core XP practice.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.why_it_exists: Tests written after the code are influenced by the implementation — you tend to write tests that verify what the code does, not what it should do. TDD forces you to think about the interface and behaviour before the implementation. Benefits: 100% coverage of code you write (by construction), tests act as executable specification, immediate feedback when you break something, drives modular design (code that's hard to test in isolation has design problems — TDD makes you fix them immediately).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.use_when: Use TDD for: algorithmic code (pricing, validation, state machines, parsers), business logic with complex rules, refactoring existing code (write tests first to capture current behaviour, then refactor). TDD is most valuable when you're building from scratch or implementing well-defined specifications.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.avoid_when: Avoid strict TDD for: UI development (hard to write meaningful unit tests for CSS/layout), exploratory/spike code (you're learning the shape of the problem — write tests after the spike), and framework boilerplate (DI registration, database migrations). TDD is a tool for code quality, not a religious obligation for all code.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_goes_wrong:
- Testing the wrong thing: writing tests that test the test framework or trivial boilerplate. TDD becomes overhead without quality gains. Each test should encode a specific behaviour rule that would catch a real bug if violated.
- Skipping refactor: teams do Red → Green then immediately move to the next feature. Code accumulates without cleanup. The Refactor step is not optional — it's where TDD pays its design dividend. Green tests give you permission to clean safely.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.real_example: A payments team implements a new fee calculation engine using TDD: 23 tests written before any production code. Each test encoded a fee rule from the business specification. The final implementation was 80 lines of code driven by 23 tests. During a regulatory change 6 months later, updating two fee rules meant changing two tests (to match new rules), fixing the implementation until tests passed, and having confidence the other 21 rules were unchanged. The TDD-built calculator had zero production incidents in 2 years; the old calculator (written without tests, ad-hoc) had 4 fee calculation incidents in the same period.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_it_is: Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD) extends TDD by centering specifications on user-visible behaviours in plain language. Instead of technical tests, BDD uses **Gherkin** scenarios — human-readable, given/when/then format that business stakeholders can write and understand. Scenarios become executable tests via frameworks: Cucumber (Java/Ruby/JS), SpecFlow (C#), Behave (Python). BDD bridges the gap between business requirements and technical implementation: a business analyst writes scenarios, a developer implements step definitions that execute the scenarios as tests.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.why_it_exists: TDD tests are written by developers in code — business stakeholders can't read or verify them. BDD makes the specification a shared artefact: business people write/review scenarios in English; developers implement step definitions; QA verifies scenarios. Dan North (BDD creator, 2006): 'BDD is about having conversations, not writing tests.' The Given/When/Then vocabulary forces precision: 'Given I am logged in' is testable; 'when the user is authenticated' is ambiguous.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.how_it_works:
```gherkin
# feature file (loan_application.feature)
Feature: Personal loan application

  Scenario: Approved application for eligible customer
    Given a customer with credit score 720 and annual income of £50,000
    And no existing loans over £5,000
    When they apply for a loan of £10,000 over 36 months
    Then the application should be approved
    And the offered interest rate should be 6.9% APR
    And the monthly payment should be £308.49

  Scenario Outline: Credit score determines eligibility
    Given a customer with credit score <score>
    When they apply for a loan of £10,000
    Then the application should be <decision>

    Examples:
      | score | decision |
      | 750   | approved |
      | 650   | approved |
      | 580   | declined |
      | 400   | declined |
```

```csharp
// SpecFlow step definitions (C#)
[Given(@"a customer with credit score (\d+) and annual income of £(\d+),(\d+)")]
public void GivenCustomerWithScoreAndIncome(int score, int thousands, int hundreds) {
    _customer = new Customer {
        CreditScore = score,
        AnnualIncome = thousands * 1000 + hundreds
    };
}

[When(@"they apply for a loan of £(\d+),(\d+) over (\d+) months")]
public void WhenTheyApplyForLoan(int thousands, int hundreds, int months) {
    _application = _loanService.Apply(_customer,
        amount: thousands * 1000 + hundreds,
        termMonths: months);
}

[Then(@"the application should be approved")]
public void ThenApplicationShouldBeApproved() =>
    Assert.Equal(LoanDecision.Approved, _application.Decision);

[Then(@"the offered interest rate should be (.*)% APR")]
public void ThenInterestRateShouldBe(decimal expectedRate) =>
    Assert.Equal(expectedRate, _application.AprRate);
```
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.use_when: Use BDD when: business stakeholders can and will participate in scenario writing (financial services, healthcare, insurance — domain rules are complex and need business validation), for acceptance test automation where traceability from business requirement to test is important, and for creating living documentation of system behaviour.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.avoid_when: Avoid BDD for: technical components without business-visible behaviour (caching layer, serialization), small teams where developer-written unit tests are sufficient, and when business stakeholders don't engage with the scenarios (Gherkin files written by developers to describe technical behaviour add overhead without the collaboration benefit).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_goes_wrong:
- Scenario explosion: teams write 500+ Gherkin scenarios covering every variant. Scenarios become slow (each scenario starts a new browser/API session), hard to maintain, and nobody reads them. Prefer 20 high-value scenarios covering key paths over 500 exhaustive scenarios.
- Step definition fragmentation: two scenarios use 'Given a logged-in user' but with slight wording differences, producing two separate step definitions. Inconsistency accumulates. Fix: maintain a shared step definition library with canonical phrases, enforce via code review.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.real_example: A UK bank uses SpecFlow for mortgage eligibility rules: 150 Gherkin scenarios written by mortgage advisors in plain English, then implemented as SpecFlow tests. When FCA changed the stress-test interest rate, the mortgage advisor updated 3 scenario examples (the new threshold values); developers updated 2 lines of step definitions; tests turned red, then green after the business logic update. The scenarios serve dual purpose: regression test suite AND FCA audit evidence ('here are the scenarios our software was tested against, signed off by our compliance team').

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_it_is: pytest is Python's dominant testing framework — simpler than unittest (no class required), more powerful (fixtures, plugins), with excellent CI integration. Key features: **fixtures** (`@pytest.fixture`) — dependency injection for tests, providing reusable setup/teardown; **parametrize** (`@pytest.mark.parametrize`) — run the same test with multiple input sets; **markers** (`@pytest.mark.slow`, `@pytest.mark.integration`) — categorise tests for selective execution; **conftest.py** — module for shared fixtures; rich plugin ecosystem (pytest-cov, pytest-asyncio, pytest-mock, pytest-django).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.why_it_exists: Python's built-in `unittest` requires inheriting from `TestCase`, verbose setup (`self.assertEqual`), and explicit test class structure. pytest makes writing tests as natural as writing functions: `def test_addition(): assert 1 + 1 == 2`. Fixtures solve test setup complexity (database connections, temp files, HTTP mocks) with scoped, reusable dependency injection — no copy-pasting setup/teardown across test classes.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.how_it_works:
```python
# conftest.py — shared fixtures across test files
import pytest
from myapp import create_app, db as _db

@pytest.fixture(scope="session")
def app():
    """Application fixture — created once per test session"""
    app = create_app(testing=True)
    with app.app_context():
        yield app

@pytest.fixture(scope="function")  # default scope — per test
def db(app):
    """Database fixture — transaction rolled back after each test"""
    _db.create_all()
    yield _db
    _db.session.rollback()
    _db.drop_all()

@pytest.fixture
def client(app):
    return app.test_client()

@pytest.fixture
def sample_user(db):
    user = User(name="Alice", email="alice@example.com")
    db.session.add(user)
    db.session.commit()
    return user

# test_pricing.py
import pytest
from myapp.pricing import calculate_discount

# Parametrize: same test, different inputs
@pytest.mark.parametrize("total,expected_discount", [
    (50.0,   0.0),   # under threshold: no discount
    (100.0,  0.0),   # at threshold: no discount
    (100.01, 0.10),  # just over: 10% discount
    (200.0,  0.10),  # well over: 10% discount
    (500.01, 0.20),  # premium threshold: 20% discount
])
def test_discount_tiers(total, expected_discount):
    assert calculate_discount(total) == expected_discount

# Markers: categorise and selectively run tests
@pytest.mark.integration
def test_order_persisted_to_db(db, sample_user):
    order = create_order(user_id=sample_user.id, amount=150.0)
    db.session.commit()
    retrieved = Order.query.filter_by(user_id=sample_user.id).first()
    assert retrieved is not None
    assert retrieved.amount == 150.0

@pytest.mark.slow
def test_bulk_import_performance(db):
    # Takes 10+ seconds
    ...

# pytest.ini — configure markers
# [pytest]
# markers =
#   slow: marks tests as slow (deselect with '-m not slow')
#   integration: marks integration tests
```

```bash
# Run only fast unit tests (exclude slow + integration)
pytest -m 'not slow and not integration'
# Run with coverage
pytest --cov=myapp --cov-report=html
# Run specific file/test
pytest tests/test_pricing.py::test_discount_tiers
```
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.use_when: Use pytest for all Python testing — unit, integration, API. Use `@pytest.fixture` for any setup reused across multiple tests (database sessions, HTTP mock servers, temp directories). Use `@pytest.mark.parametrize` for boundary value tests and equivalence partitions. Use markers to separate fast unit tests from slow integration tests for CI optimisation.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.avoid_when: Avoid `unittest.TestCase` (verbose, class-required) when pytest is available. Avoid fixtures with `scope='session'` for tests that modify shared state — use `scope='function'` with transaction rollback to ensure test isolation.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_goes_wrong:
- Fixture scope misuse: `scope='session'` shared database state that one test modifies causes subtle failures in later tests. Always use `scope='function'` for database fixtures and roll back transactions after each test.
- `conftest.py` coupling: a single `conftest.py` with 50 fixtures becomes a shared global state nightmare. Organise `conftest.py` files per test directory, with only truly shared fixtures in the root conftest.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.real_example: FastAPI service's test suite: `conftest.py` defines `async_client` fixture (httpx `AsyncClient` wrapping the FastAPI app), `db_session` fixture (async SQLAlchemy session with rollback), and `mock_redis` fixture (fakeredis instance). Pricing tests: 20 `@pytest.mark.parametrize` cases for tier boundaries. Running `pytest -m 'not integration'` runs 800 unit tests in 4 seconds in CI; `pytest -m integration` runs 200 integration tests against a TestContainers PostgreSQL in 90 seconds (run only on main branch merge).

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_it_is: JUnit (Java) and xUnit (C#) are the dominant unit testing frameworks for their respective ecosystems. **JUnit 5** (Jupiter): `@Test`, `@BeforeEach`, `@AfterEach`, `@ParameterizedTest`, `@ExtendWith` for extension points (Spring, Mockito). **xUnit.net** (C#): convention-based (`[Fact]` for single test, `[Theory]` + `[InlineData]`/`[MemberData]` for parameterised), `IClassFixture<T>` for shared state, `IAsyncLifetime` for async setup/teardown. Both follow the AAA pattern (Arrange-Act-Assert) and integrate with CI via test result XML (JUnit format, universally supported).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.why_it_exists: Java had JUnit since 1997 (Kent Beck + Erich Gamma) — it pioneered the xUnit pattern that all modern test frameworks follow. xUnit.net (Brad Wilson, James Newkirk) brought the pattern to .NET with refinements: no shared `[Setup]`/`[TearDown]` methods (isolation via constructor injection), `[Theory]` for data-driven tests, no test runner coupling. Both are test execution frameworks — they don't provide mocking (use Mockito for Java, Moq/NSubstitute for C#) or assertion libraries (AssertJ for Java, Shouldly/FluentAssertions for C#).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.use_when: Use JUnit 5 for all Java tests (preferred over JUnit 4 — `@ExtendWith` is more flexible than `@RunWith`). Use xUnit for .NET (preferred over NUnit or MSTest for new projects — cleaner isolation model). Both are industry standard and have excellent IDE and CI support.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.avoid_when: Avoid mixing test frameworks in one project (JUnit + TestNG, xUnit + NUnit) — pick one and standardise. Avoid `@BeforeClass`/static setup in JUnit (shares state between tests — use `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)` intentionally when shared state is needed).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.what_goes_wrong:
- xUnit test isolation: xUnit creates a new instance of the test class for each `[Fact]`. This is intentional (prevents shared state). Code that relies on field state set by a previous test will fail non-deterministically as xUnit doesn't guarantee test order. Each test must be self-contained via `[Fact]` constructor setup or `IClassFixture<T>`.
- JUnit 5 extension conflicts: `@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)` and `@ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class)` can conflict. Use `@SpringBootTest` which includes the Spring extension; add `@MockBean` for mocks within Spring tests.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|Testing Practi.real_example: Spring Boot microservice CI pipeline: 1,200 JUnit 5 unit tests run in 15 seconds (Maven Surefire). 200 integration tests with `@SpringBootTest` + TestContainers run in 3 minutes (Maven Failsafe). On every PR: unit tests (fast gate, blocking). Nightly: full integration suite. xUnit .NET service: 800 `[Fact]` + `[Theory]` tests in 8 seconds. `IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>` provides one test server per class, `IAsyncLifetime` handles database seeding/cleanup per test. Both frameworks generate JUnit XML results consumed by GitHub Actions for test result visualisation.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_it_is: REST (Representational State Transfer, Roy Fielding 2000) is an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems. Key constraints: stateless (each request contains all information needed), client-server, cacheable, uniform interface. In practice: **Resources** — nouns in URLs (`/orders`, `/users/123`, `/orders/5/items`). **HTTP verbs** — `GET` (read), `POST` (create), `PUT` (full replace), `PATCH` (partial update), `DELETE` (delete). **Status codes** — `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`, `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `403 Forbidden`, `404 Not Found`, `409 Conflict`, `422 Unprocessable Entity`, `500 Internal Server Error`. **Versioning** — URL prefix (`/v1/orders`), Accept header, or query param.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.why_it_exists: Before REST, APIs used RPC-style or SOAP endpoints (`/getUserById?id=123`, WSDL contracts, XML envelopes). REST leverages HTTP's existing semantics (verbs, status codes, caching headers) rather than reinventing them. A `GET /orders/123` is intuitively safe (no side effects) and cacheable; a `DELETE /orders/123` is intuitively destructive. HTTP clients, proxies, CDNs, and browsers all understand these semantics natively.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.how_it_works:
```
=== Resource design ===
Collection:  GET  /orders          → list orders
Single:      GET  /orders/{id}     → get one order
Create:      POST /orders          → create order (request body: new order data)
Update:      PUT  /orders/{id}     → replace order (full body required)
Partial:     PATCH /orders/{id}    → update fields (partial body)
Delete:      DELETE /orders/{id}   → delete order
Nested:      GET  /orders/{id}/items → items for an order

=== HTTP status codes ===
GET /orders/123 — order found: 200 with body
GET /orders/999 — not found:   404
POST /orders    — created:     201 with Location: /orders/456 header
DELETE /orders/123 — deleted:  204 (no body)
POST /orders (invalid data): 422 Unprocessable Entity
POST /orders (auth required): 401 Unauthorized
POST /orders (auth ok, no permission): 403 Forbidden
POST /orders (duplicate): 409 Conflict

=== Versioning strategies ===
URL prefix:     /api/v1/orders  (most common, explicit)
Accept header:  Accept: application/vnd.myapi.v2+json
Query param:    /api/orders?version=2

=== Response envelope ===
// Single resource:
{ "id": 123, "status": "pending", "total": 99.99 }

// Collection with pagination:
{
  "data": [{ ... }, { ... }],
  "pagination": {
    "total": 1000, "page": 2, "pageSize": 20,
    "nextUrl": "/api/v1/orders?page=3&pageSize=20"
  }
}

// Error:
{ "error": "VALIDATION_ERROR", "message": "Amount must be positive",
  "details": [{ "field": "amount", "code": "NEGATIVE" }] }
```
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.use_when: Use REST for: public APIs (widely understood by all HTTP clients), CRUD-heavy services (orders, users, products), APIs consumed by web/mobile clients, and when cacheability and discoverability matter. REST is the default — use it unless you have specific reasons for GraphQL (flexible querying) or gRPC (streaming, high performance, internal services).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.avoid_when: Avoid REST for: complex queries requiring client-specific data shapes (GraphQL is better), real-time streaming (WebSockets or gRPC streaming), RPC-style operations that don't map to CRUD (e.g., 'run a report', 'merge two accounts' — though these can be modelled as POST /reports, POST /account-merges).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_goes_wrong:
- Verb/noun confusion: `POST /createOrder` (RPC-style, verb in URL) vs `POST /orders` (REST-style, noun). REST uses nouns for resources and HTTP verbs for actions — mixing verbs into URLs creates inconsistency that confuses API consumers.
- Wrong status codes: returning `200 OK` for errors (Twitter's classic mistake: `{ 'error': 'not found' }` with `200 OK`) breaks HTTP clients that use status codes for error detection. Using `500 Internal Server Error` for validation failures (client's fault, not server's) incorrectly signals server issues — use `400` family for client errors, `500` family for server errors.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.real_example: GitHub's REST API: `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues` (list issues), `POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues` (create issue), `PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}` (update issue), `DELETE /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number}/labels/{name}` (remove label). Consistent versioning via `Accept: application/vnd.github.v3+json`. Status codes: `201 Created` on issue creation with `Location` header pointing to the new issue URL. Well-documented, versioned, consistent — a frequently cited REST API design reference.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_it_is: Advanced REST design conventions beyond basic CRUD. **HATEOAS** (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State): responses include links to related actions the client can take next — `{ 'id': 123, 'status': 'pending', '_links': { 'pay': {'href': '/orders/123/payment'}, 'cancel': {'href': '/orders/123/cancel'} } }`. Clients discover API navigation dynamically rather than hardcoding URLs. **Pagination**: large collections returned in pages — cursor-based (`?cursor=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ`) or offset-based (`?page=2&pageSize=20`). **Filtering/Sorting**: `GET /orders?status=pending&minTotal=100&sort=-createdAt` (minus = descending).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.why_it_exists: HATEOAS: API clients that hardcode URLs break when the server changes URL structure. With HATEOAS, clients follow links from the root resource — the API is self-describing. Pagination: returning 1M orders in a single response exhausts memory and bandwidth. Cursor-based pagination is stable (no missing/duplicate items when records are inserted/deleted); offset-based is simpler but can skip items. Filtering: clients need subsets of data without fetching everything and filtering client-side.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.use_when: Use cursor-based pagination for feeds and live data (Instagram, Twitter timelines). Use offset-based for admin UIs with explicit page numbers. Use filtering for any collection endpoint that could grow beyond 100 items. HATEOAS is valuable for APIs that change frequently or APIs with complex state machines where valid next actions depend on current state.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.avoid_when: Avoid HATEOAS for internal APIs consumed by a single client you control — the overhead of link embedding without the benefit of client-server decoupling isn't worth it. Avoid offset pagination for real-time data (page 2 returns different items if new records were added between page 1 and page 2 requests).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_goes_wrong:
- Unbounded collection endpoints: `GET /orders` that returns all orders without pagination — works in development (100 orders), times out in production (100,000 orders). Always add `?limit=` with a max cap (e.g., max 100) and return pagination metadata.
- Filter injection: `GET /orders?sql=DROP TABLE orders` — naive filter implementations that pass query params directly to SQL. Always whitelist allowed filter fields and use parameterised queries.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.real_example: Stripe API uses cursor-based pagination with `starting_after` and `ending_before` parameters: `GET /v1/charges?limit=10&starting_after=ch_previous_id`. Each response includes `has_more: true/false` and the last item's `id` as the next cursor. This ensures that even if new charges are created during pagination (which happens constantly on Stripe), you never miss or duplicate a charge. Stripe's pagination design is widely cited as the reference implementation.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_it_is: GraphQL is a query language for APIs (Facebook, 2015) and a runtime for executing those queries. Clients specify exactly the data shape they need: `query { user(id: 123) { name email orders(last: 5) { id total status } } }` — one request, exactly the fields needed, from nested resources. Three operation types: **Query** (read data), **Mutation** (write data), **Subscription** (real-time push via WebSocket). **Schema**: GraphQL is strongly typed — a schema defines all types, queries, mutations, and their fields.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.why_it_exists: REST APIs suffer from over-fetching (endpoint returns 50 fields, client uses 3) and under-fetching (need 5 separate REST requests to compose one screen's data). Mobile apps on slow networks pay the cost of both. GraphQL solves these: one request, exactly the fields needed, from multiple resources in one roundtrip. Facebook built GraphQL for its mobile news feed — hundreds of different data shapes needed by different parts of the feed, all served from one GraphQL endpoint.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.use_when: Use GraphQL for: mobile apps needing flexible, minimal data fetching, front-end teams who need self-service data (query exactly what they need without backend changes), products with many different UI surfaces needing different data shapes from the same data model, and when real-time subscriptions are required alongside queries.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.avoid_when: Avoid GraphQL for: simple REST-suitable CRUD services, file uploads (REST multipart is simpler), public APIs where HTTP caching is critical (GraphQL POST requests aren't cached by default), and teams new to API development (REST is simpler to learn, debug, and monitor). GraphQL N+1 query problems require DataLoader — additional complexity.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_goes_wrong:
- N+1 query problem: querying `orders { customer { name } }` — GraphQL naively resolves `customer` for each order with a separate query: 1 query for orders + N queries for customers. Fix: DataLoader (batches N customer queries into 1: `SELECT * FROM customers WHERE id IN (1,2,3,...)`). Every field resolver that fetches related data must use DataLoader in production.
- Schema sprawl: GraphQL schemas grow organically to 500+ types. Without governance, different teams add duplicate types (`UserV1`, `UserNew`), deprecated fields accumulate, and schema documentation becomes stale. Use GraphQL introspection for documentation and a schema registry for governance.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.real_example: GitHub migrated to GraphQL for their v4 API: developers querying PR data used to need 5+ REST requests (PR details, review comments, status checks, commit SHA, labels). With GraphQL: one query fetches all of it with exactly the fields the client needs. GitHub's GraphQL API serves millions of queries daily from CI/CD tools, IDE extensions, and third-party apps. The schema has 300+ types and is publicly documented via introspection.

15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_it_is: gRPC is Google's high-performance Remote Procedure Call framework using Protocol Buffers (protobuf) for serialization. Services are defined in `.proto` files: `rpc GetOrder(GetOrderRequest) returns (Order)`. `protoc` generates client and server code in 10+ languages. Communication uses HTTP/2 (multiplexing, header compression, binary framing). Four types: **Unary** (request/response), **Server streaming** (one request, stream of responses), **Client streaming** (stream of requests, one response), **Bidirectional streaming** (both sides stream). Default: binary protobuf serialization (5-10× smaller than JSON, 2-10× faster to parse).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.why_it_exists: REST/JSON for internal microservice communication is verbose (JSON parsing overhead, large payloads), loosely typed (no schema enforcement), and HTTP/1.1 limited (one request per connection). gRPC solves these for internal services: binary protobuf is compact and fast, `.proto` schema enforces contracts (compile-time type safety), HTTP/2 multiplexes multiple RPCs on one connection, and generated clients eliminate handwritten HTTP client code.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.use_when: Use gRPC for: internal microservice-to-microservice communication (lower latency, smaller payloads than REST/JSON), real-time bidirectional streaming (live tracking, telemetry), polyglot environments (one .proto generates clients in Go, Python, Java, C#), and performance-critical internal APIs. Kubernetes-native services use gRPC internally for 2-5× lower latency than REST.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.avoid_when: Avoid gRPC for: public APIs (browser support limited — grpc-web required, complex proxy setup), APIs consumed by human users (REST/JSON is more debuggable with curl), and simple CRUD without streaming needs (REST is simpler to build and test). gRPC is powerful but has significant operational overhead (HTTP/2 load balancing, certificate management, tracing setup).
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.what_goes_wrong:
- HTTP/2 load balancing: L4 load balancers (AWS ALB in TCP mode) don't see individual HTTP/2 frames — they pin all gRPC calls from one client to one server (no per-RPC load balancing). Fix: use Envoy/Istio service mesh for L7 gRPC-aware load balancing, or client-side load balancing.
- Proto backward compatibility: removing a field from a `.proto` or changing a field number breaks all clients generated from the old proto. Follow proto evolution rules: never remove field numbers (mark deprecated instead), only add optional fields, never change field types.
15|🔴 T1 Testing & Quality|APIs & System.real_example: Google's internal infrastructure uses gRPC for all service-to-service communication — Kubernetes itself uses gRPC (etcd uses gRPC, kubelet communicates with API server via gRPC). In a .NET microservices system: the `OrderService` calls `InventoryService` via gRPC (unary RPC, 3× lower latency than REST/JSON), and the `AnalyticsService` consumes an order stream via server-streaming RPC (`StreamOrders`). REST endpoints face externally to mobile apps; gRPC is internal — chosen specifically for the performance-critical inventory reservation path.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_it_is: Git stores everything as four types of content-addressable objects, identified by SHA-1 hashes: **Blob**: stores file content (no filename, just content). **Tree**: directory — lists blobs (files) and subtrees (subdirectories) with names and permissions. **Commit**: points to a tree (root directory snapshot), has parent commit(s), author/committer, and message. **Tag**: annotated pointer to a commit with tagger info. All objects are immutable and content-addressed: the SHA-1 hash of an object IS its address. Two files with identical content share one blob. This is why Git is fast — it's a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of immutable content-addressed objects.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.why_it_exists: Git's content-addressed object model enables: **integrity** (any corruption changes the hash, detectable), **deduplication** (same content = same hash = stored once), **efficient branching** (a branch is just a pointer to a commit hash — creating a branch is O(1)), **merging** (find common ancestor commit, merge DAGs). Linus Torvalds designed Git for the Linux kernel: thousands of contributors, millions of files, needed to be fast and distributed with no central server required.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.how_it_works:
```bash
# Inspect git objects
git cat-file -t HEAD          # type of HEAD commit → 'commit'
git cat-file -p HEAD          # content of HEAD commit
# tree 4b825dc642cb6eb9a060e54bf8d69288fbee4904   ← root tree object
# parent abc123...                                  ← previous commit
# author Alice <alice@example.com> 1718000000 +0000
# committer Alice <alice@example.com> 1718000000 +0000
#
# Add user authentication feature

git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}   # content of root tree
# 100644 blob a8c3... README.md
# 040000 tree b2f1... src/
# 100755 blob c9e2... run.sh

git cat-file -p HEAD^{tree}:src  # content of src/ subtree
# 100644 blob d1a3... main.py
# 100644 blob e2b4... models.py

git cat-file -s HEAD           # size of HEAD commit in bytes

# Branching is just pointer manipulation:
git log --oneline --graph --all  # visualise DAG

# A branch = file in .git/refs/heads/ containing a commit hash:
cat .git/refs/heads/main        # → abc123...
# Creating a branch: create a new file with the same hash
git branch feature/auth        # → creates .git/refs/heads/feature/auth with content = HEAD hash
# COST: O(1) regardless of repo size — just writes a hash to a file

# Merge = create a commit with two parents:
git log --pretty=format:'%H %P %s' # %P = parent hashes
# merge commits show two parent hashes
```
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.use_when: Understand Git internals for: debugging merge conflicts (trace common ancestor via `git merge-base`), recovering 'lost' commits (nothing is deleted until GC runs, find by `git reflog` or `git fsck`), understanding why operations are O(1) (branches) vs O(n) (log), and teaching Git effectively. Also needed for: writing Git hooks, custom Git tooling, and troubleshooting corrupted repos.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.avoid_when: No need to manually manipulate git objects for normal development workflow. Use porcelain commands (`git commit`, `git merge`, `git log`) for daily work. Understand internals for debugging and tooling, not for everyday usage.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_goes_wrong:
- Assuming 'git delete branch' deletes code: deleting a branch deletes the pointer, not the commits. Commits are reachable until GC (`git gc --prune`) runs. Use `git reflog` to recover recently deleted branches: `git checkout -b recovered-branch <SHA-from-reflog>`.
- SHA collision concerns: Git uses SHA-1, which has known theoretical collisions (SHAttered, 2017). GitHub and recent Git versions (2.39+) support SHA-256 (`--object-format=sha256`) for new repositories. In practice, accidental SHA-1 collision probability is negligible for normal repositories.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.real_example: GitHub's code search: indexes all Git blobs by SHA-1 hash. The same blob SHA in 1000 different repos is stored once in their object store and indexed once — deduplication at petabyte scale. Common open-source libraries (lodash, React) appear as blobs across millions of forks: one blob storage entry per unique file version, not per fork. Git's content-addressed model makes GitHub's storage economics possible.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_it_is: Three dominant Git branching strategies for team development: **Git Flow** (Vincent Driessen, 2010): `main` (production-ready), `develop` (integration), feature branches (`feature/x` from develop), release branches (`release/1.0` from develop), hotfix branches (`hotfix/1.0.1` from main). Structured, suited for release-based delivery. **Trunk-Based Development (TBD)**: everyone commits to `main` (the 'trunk') with short-lived feature branches (≤1 day). Feature flags hide incomplete features. Requires comprehensive CI. **GitHub Flow**: simplified — only `main` + short feature branches. PR → review → merge to main → deploy.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.why_it_exists: Without a branching strategy, teams have conflicts, unclear 'source of truth', and unpredictable releases. Each strategy optimises for different release cadences: Git Flow for versioned software with scheduled releases (libraries, apps with quarterly releases); TBD for continuous delivery (web apps deploying multiple times per day); GitHub Flow for teams deploying on merge (simpler than Git Flow, faster than TBD with more structure).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.how_it_works:
```bash
# === Git Flow ===
# Feature development
git checkout develop
git checkout -b feature/user-auth
# ... develop ...
git checkout develop && git merge --no-ff feature/user-auth
git branch -d feature/user-auth

# Release
git checkout -b release/1.2 develop
# ... final testing, version bumps ...
git checkout main && git merge --no-ff release/1.2
git tag -a v1.2.0
git checkout develop && git merge --no-ff release/1.2

# Hotfix
git checkout -b hotfix/1.2.1 main
# ... fix ...
git checkout main && git merge --no-ff hotfix/1.2.1
git tag -a v1.2.1
git checkout develop && git merge --no-ff hotfix/1.2.1

# === Trunk-Based Development ===
# Short-lived feature branch (≤1 day)
git checkout -b feat/add-login  # from main
# ... develop, keep small ...
git checkout main && git merge feat/add-login  # or PR
git push origin main  # triggers deploy
# Use feature flags for incomplete features:
# if (featureFlags.IsEnabled('new-checkout')) { ... }
```

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.use_when: Use **Git Flow** for: versioned libraries/SDKs, mobile apps with app store releases, enterprise software with formal release cycles. Use **GitHub Flow** for: small teams, SaaS apps without complex release requirements. Use **TBD** for: high-frequency deployment (10+ deploys/day), mature CI/CD teams, when merge conflicts are a bottleneck.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.avoid_when: Avoid Git Flow for: continuous delivery web apps — the ceremony (release branches, develop branch) slows deployment velocity. Avoid TBD without comprehensive test coverage and feature flags — deploying incomplete features to production is dangerous without a way to hide them.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_goes_wrong:
- Long-lived feature branches: a branch alive for 3 weeks accumulates 'merge debt' — reintegrating it against main requires resolving hundreds of conflicts. TBD addresses this with daily integration; Git Flow's `develop` branch address this with daily merges from features. The anti-pattern is feature branches that live as long as the feature takes to build (weeks/months).
- Hotfix deployed without merging back: a Git Flow hotfix merged to main but not back to develop means the same bug appears in the next release from develop. Git Flow requires merging hotfixes to both main and develop — easy to forget under production pressure.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.real_example: Google Chrome: Trunk-Based Development on a single `main` branch. 1000+ engineers commit daily. Feature flags control which features appear in which Chrome release channel (Canary → Beta → Stable). An incomplete feature can be in main for months behind a flag, never visible to users until the flag is enabled for a release. Contrast with Linux kernel: Git Flow-style with Linus's `master` + integration branches (`net-next`, `drm-next`) that merge into `next` before being pulled to `master` for each kernel release.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_it_is: Two strategies for integrating changes from one branch into another. **Merge** (`git merge feature`): creates a new 'merge commit' with two parents — preserves the complete history of both branches. The commit graph shows when branches diverged and when they rejoined (true reflection of development history). **Rebase** (`git rebase main`): re-applies feature branch commits on top of main, as if the feature was developed from main's current tip. Produces a linear history without merge commits. Golden rule: never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared remote branch (it rewrites history, causing divergence for others).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.why_it_exists: Different teams have different history preferences: **merge** gives complete, accurate history (who developed what, when branches split and merged — useful for forensics). **Rebase** gives clean linear history that's easier to read with `git log --oneline` and simpler to bisect with `git bisect`. Neither is universally correct — the choice is about what history model the team values.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.how_it_works:
```bash
# === Merge ===
# On feature branch:
git checkout main
git merge feature/auth
# Creates: O---O---O---M (M = merge commit with two parents)
#              \       /
#               A---B  (feature commits)

# git log shows:
# M: Merge branch 'feature/auth'
# B: Add JWT token validation
# A: Add login endpoint
# O: Previous main commit (interleaved with A, B by time)

git log --oneline --graph
# * M  Merge branch 'feature/auth'
# |\   
# | * B  Add JWT validation
# | * A  Add login endpoint
# * O  Previous main work

# === Rebase ===
# On feature branch:
git checkout feature/auth
git rebase main
# Replays A, B on top of latest main:
# O---O---O---A'---B' (A', B' = rebased copies of A, B)
# Then merge (fast-forward):
git checkout main && git merge feature/auth  # fast-forward, no merge commit

# git log shows perfectly linear history:
# B'  Add JWT validation
# A'  Add login endpoint
# O   Previous main work

# === Interactive rebase (squash, reorder, edit) ===
git rebase -i HEAD~3  # rebase last 3 commits interactively
# pick a1b2c3 Add login endpoint
# squash d4e5f6 WIP: auth  ← squash into previous
# squash g7h8i9 Fix typo   ← squash into previous
# → results in one clean commit 'Add login endpoint'

# NEVER do:
git push origin main
git rebase main  # rewrites pushed commits → force push needed → team diverges
```
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.use_when: Use **merge** for: integrating long-running branches where the history of when the branch was active matters (release branches, hotfixes), shared branches where others have based work on your commits, and when team policy favours complete history. Use **rebase** for: cleaning up local commits before PR review (squash WIP commits), keeping feature branch current with main during development (`git rebase main` while you work), and when team prefers linear history.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.avoid_when: Never rebase commits that have been pushed to a shared branch that others have pulled from — their local history diverges, requiring `git pull --rebase` or `git reset --hard`. The rule: rebase local commits freely; never rebase pushed commits (unless everyone on the team knows and agrees to force-pull).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_goes_wrong:
- Lost commits after rebase: `git rebase --interactive` with `drop` removes commits. If you drop a commit with meaningful work, use `git reflog` to find the original SHA and `git cherry-pick` it back. Nothing is truly lost until GC runs.
- Rebase conflicts vs merge conflicts: rebasing a 20-commit feature branch requires resolving conflicts per-commit (you may resolve the same conflict 20 times). Merging resolves conflicts once (at the merge point). For large long-lived branches, merge is often less painful — the single merge conflict is simpler than 20 sequential rebase conflicts.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.real_example: Linux kernel: Linus Torvalds uses merge commits exclusively — the kernel's commit graph shows every integration point, when subsystems merged, and who maintained what. `git log --graph` of the kernel shows a river delta of branches merging into Linus's main tree. This is deliberate: the kernel's history is a legal and historical record. Contrast: most open-source projects (React, Vue, TypeScript) require PRs to be rebased/squashed before merge — GitHub's 'Squash and Merge' button is the canonical example of rebase-style linear history enforcement.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_it_is: A Pull Request (PR) / Merge Request (MR) is a mechanism to propose, discuss, review, and integrate code changes. The author: creates a feature branch, pushes commits, opens a PR with description. Reviewers: inspect the diff, comment on specific lines, request changes, approve. CI runs automated checks (tests, linting, security scanning). The PR merges when: all CI checks pass + required approvals received. Code review is the practice of reviewers examining the PR diff for: correctness, security vulnerabilities, performance issues, test coverage, adherence to team conventions, and maintainability.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.why_it_exists: Unreviewed code entering main branches: introduces bugs caught only in production, propagates anti-patterns across the codebase, and makes individuals the sole owners of knowledge (no team awareness). PRs create: quality gates (peer review catches bugs before they ship), knowledge sharing (reviewers learn about the feature, authors learn review feedback), documentation (PR description + comments are future context for git blame), and audit trails (compliance/security requirements).

```
✓ Tests: are edge cases covered? Is coverage meaningful?
```

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.use_when: Always use PRs for: code going into shared branches (main, develop), security-sensitive code (auth, payment, PII handling), public API changes, infrastructure changes, and any change with production impact. Set required reviewers (at minimum 1, preferably 2 for critical paths). Automate what you can: linting, tests, coverage checks — reviewers should focus on logic and design, not style.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.avoid_when: Avoid PRs for: solo projects with no team, emergency production hotfixes where time constraint overrides process (document the bypass, review post-merge), and trivially automated changes (dependency bumps by Dependabot reviewed by automated CI, not humans). Don't let PR reviews become rubber-stamping — two approvals from people who didn't read the code is worse than one thorough review.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.what_goes_wrong:
- Review-as-bottleneck: PRs sitting for 3+ days waiting for review. Solution: make review a team norm (SLA: 1 business day), use async communication (DM reviewers, not just 'assigned in GitHub'), and keep PRs small (< 400 lines changed is reviewable; > 1000 lines becomes rubber-stamping).
- Style comments crowding out logic review: reviewers spend 80% of review comments on indentation and naming, zero time on logic correctness. Fix: automate style with linters and formatters (pre-commit hooks, CI). Reviewers should only comment on what automation can't catch: logic, security, architecture.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|Git & C.real_example: Google's engineering culture requires every code change to be reviewed by at least one person who is not the author, using the Critique code review tool (internal equivalent of Gerrit). Google's 'Readability' program: engineers must demonstrate code review mastery in each language to merge code without a 'Readability Mentor' co-approving. This enforces consistency across millions of lines of code by thousands of engineers. The PR process is the primary code quality control mechanism at Google-scale — not just a collaboration tool.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_it_is: Continuous Integration (CI) is the practice of automatically building and testing code every time a developer commits to the shared repository. On every `git push` to any branch: a CI server (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins, CircleCI) runs: (1) compile/build, (2) unit tests, (3) integration tests, (4) linting/code style, (5) security scanning. If any step fails, the commit is flagged; the developer fixes before merging. Martin Fowler: 'The key test is that you should be able to walk in to any developer and, in a couple of minutes, have their machine checked out, compiling, and running tests.'
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.why_it_exists: Without CI, integration problems accumulate: developer A's code and developer B's code work independently but fail together — discovered only when someone manually tries to merge everything at the end of the sprint ('integration hell'). CI surfaces these conflicts within minutes of the commit — while context is fresh and the change is small. Additionally, manual builds are error-prone ('works on my machine') — CI provides a clean, reproducible build environment.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.how_it_works:
```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (GitHub Actions)
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, develop]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test, POSTGRES_DB: testdb }
        options: --health-cmd pg_isready --health-interval 10s

    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Setup .NET
        uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '9.x' }

      - name: Restore
        run: dotnet restore

      - name: Build
        run: dotnet build --no-restore --configuration Release

      - name: Unit tests
        run: dotnet test --no-build --filter 'Category!=Integration' --configuration Release

      - name: Integration tests
        run: dotnet test --no-build --filter 'Category=Integration' --configuration Release
        env:
          ConnectionStrings__Default: Server=localhost;Database=testdb;User=postgres;Password=test

      - name: Upload coverage
        uses: codecov/codecov-action@v3

  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Lint
        run: dotnet format --verify-no-changes

  security:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: SAST scan
        uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
```
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.use_when: Always use CI. Every professional software project should have CI — it's table stakes, not an advanced practice. Minimum CI pipeline: build + unit tests (must be fast, <5 minutes). Extended: integration tests, code coverage, linting, security scanning. Set PRs to require all CI checks pass before merge (branch protection rules).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.avoid_when: Avoid CI pipelines so slow they're bypassed — a 45-minute CI run will be skipped under deadline pressure, negating its value. Optimise for speed: parallel jobs, test splitting, Docker layer caching. The ideal CI pipeline: <10 minutes for the PR check, full suite running in parallel.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_goes_wrong:
- Flaky tests in CI: tests that pass locally but fail intermittently in CI (timing issues, environment differences, test order dependencies). Each flaky test erodes trust in CI — teams start ignoring failures ('oh that one flakes sometimes'). Fix flaky tests immediately; they have zero value and negative ROI (false alarms waste everyone's time).
- 'Works on my machine': CI environment differs from developer machines — different OS, different tool versions, different environment variables. Fix: run CI in Docker containers matching production; use devcontainers for local development; pin all tool versions in CI configuration.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.real_example: Etsy introduced Continuous Integration in 2009, famous for running 50+ deploys per day at a time when weekly releases were industry standard. Their key insight: the discipline of CI (all code must pass build + tests before merge) forced them to keep builds fast and tests reliable. When a build breaks at Etsy, fixing it becomes the #1 priority — broken main blocks everyone. This culture made CI effective: not just tooling, but a team commitment that no broken build waits more than 10 minutes.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_it_is: Continuous Delivery (CD) extends CI: every successful build produces a deployable artifact (Docker image, .zip, .exe, Helm chart) that could be deployed to production at any time — but deployment to production requires a manual approval step. The pipeline: CI (build + test) → staging deploy (automated) → automated acceptance tests in staging → ✅ 'this artifact is production-ready' → manual deploy trigger. Jez Humble and David Farley (book: Continuous Delivery, 2010): 'Your software is deployment-ready throughout its lifecycle.' Not to be confused with Continuous Deployment (automatic to production, no manual step).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.why_it_exists: Without CD, deployments are big-bang events: months of changes accumulated, manual deployment scripts, long deployment weekends, and high failure rates (too many changes at once). CD turns deployment from a risky event into a routine activity: small changes, fully tested, always ready. Teams can deploy a feature within hours of merge rather than waiting for the next quarterly release window. Even if you don't deploy continuously, having the ability to deploy any commit on demand is transformative for incident response.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.how_it_works:
```yaml
# GitHub Actions: CI → staging → manual production gate
name: CD Pipeline

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          tags: myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          push: true

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build-and-push
    environment: staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to staging
        run: |
          helm upgrade myapp ./chart \
            --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }} \
            --namespace staging

  acceptance-tests:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run smoke tests against staging
        run: pytest tests/acceptance/ --base-url=https://staging.myapp.com

  deploy-production:
    needs: acceptance-tests
    environment:  # GitHub environment with required_reviewers = 1 approver
      name: production
      url: https://myapp.com
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: |
          helm upgrade myapp ./chart \
            --set image.tag=${{ github.sha }} \
            --namespace production

# 'deploy-production' requires a human to click 'Approve' in GitHub Actions UI
# This is the manual gate that distinguishes CD from Continuous Deployment
```
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.use_when: Use Continuous Delivery when: regulatory requirements mandate approval gates (SOX, HIPAA, FedRAMP), product needs human review of every production change, or team is not yet confident in automated acceptance test coverage for fully automatic deployment. CD is the right default for most enterprise software.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.avoid_when: Avoid CD if the manual approval gate becomes a rubber-stamp bottleneck ('someone approves everything without looking' — defeats the purpose). In that case, invest in acceptance test coverage and move to Continuous Deployment. Don't use CD as an excuse not to improve automation.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_goes_wrong:
- Deployment artifact drift: CI builds a Docker image (`sha-abc123`), staging tests pass, but production deployment uses a different version (`latest` tag that was overwritten). Always deploy the exact same artifact (by digest or immutable SHA tag) that was tested in staging. 'Works in staging' must mean the identical byte-for-byte artifact is deployed to production.
- Manual gate as unlimited holding pen: artifacts 'ready for production' accumulate without being deployed. Changes batch up, defeating the purpose of CD. Establish a deployment SLA: production deployable artifacts must be deployed within 24 hours or the team must document why not.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.real_example: Amazon's deployment pipeline (from 'The Phoenix Project' and AWS talks): every code change that passes the pipeline is automatically staged. Production deployments require approval from a 'Deployment Pipeline Owner' who reviews the automated test results. Amazon deploys to production thousands of times per day — but each deploy is a small, independently tested change. The total automation (CI → staging → automated tests) means the human approval step is validating dashboards, not re-testing manually.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_it_is: Continuous Deployment takes Continuous Delivery one step further: every commit that passes automated tests is automatically deployed to production without any manual approval gate. Pipeline: code push → CI (build + test) → staging deploy → automated acceptance tests → ✅ automatic production deploy. Netflix, Facebook, Amazon, Etsy operate with continuous deployment — code goes from developer laptop to production in minutes. The key enabler: comprehensive automated test coverage and feature flags to hide incomplete features.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.why_it_exists: Manual approval gates create bottlenecks and delays. If automated tests are comprehensive enough to give confidence, why require a human to click 'approve'? Continuous Deployment reduces lead time (time from commit to production) to minutes. Smaller, more frequent deployments are safer — each deployment is one small change, easier to roll back, easier to diagnose if it causes an incident. The 'if it's scary, do it more often' principle: deploys become routine, not events.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.how_it_works:
```yaml
# GitHub Actions: Continuous Deployment (no manual gate)
name: Deploy

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - name: Build, test, publish
        run: |
          dotnet test --configuration Release
          dotnet publish -c Release -o ./publish

  deploy-production:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        run: |
          # Deploy automatically — no human approval
          kubectl set image deployment/myapp myapp=myapp:${{ github.sha }}
          kubectl rollout status deployment/myapp --timeout=5m

      - name: Verify deployment
        run: |
          # Automated smoke test against production
          curl -f https://api.myapp.com/health
          pytest tests/smoke/ --base-url=https://api.myapp.com

      - name: Auto-rollback on failure
        if: failure()
        run: kubectl rollout undo deployment/myapp

# Safety mechanisms enabling continuous deployment:
# 1. Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Flagsmith): incomplete features hidden
# 2. Canary deployments: 5% of traffic → validate → 100%
# 3. Automated rollback: deploy fails → revert automatically
# 4. Comprehensive test suite: unit + integration + smoke tests
```
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.use_when: Use Continuous Deployment for: web services with high deployment frequency, teams with comprehensive automated test coverage (>80% meaningful coverage), when feature flags enable deploying incomplete features safely, and when your team measures DORA metrics and targets elite performance (multiple deploys per day, <1 hour lead time).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.avoid_when: Avoid Continuous Deployment for: regulated environments requiring human sign-off (SOX, PCI, HIPAA, FDA), safety-critical systems (avionics, medical devices), mobile app releases (app store review process makes CD impossible for client code), and teams without sufficient automated test coverage to trust the pipeline.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_goes_wrong:
- 'Continuous deployment' without feature flags: a half-finished feature gets deployed because it passed tests (tests don't test 'feature is complete'). Feature flags are mandatory — every in-progress feature behind a flag, disabled in production.
- Monitoring/alerting gaps: deployment succeeds (application starts), but a silent regression is introduced (a query returns wrong results, an API returns subtly wrong values). Without production monitoring (synthetic monitoring, error rate alerts, business metric anomaly detection), the regression isn't caught for hours/days.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.real_example: Etsy (engineering blog, 2010s): 'If it hurts, do it more often.' Etsy deployed 25+ times per day, every engineer could deploy, deployment was a single command. The safety net: Etsy deployed with a 'dark launch' (deploy code, but feature flag off → no users affected), then a 'ramp' (1% → 10% → 50% → 100% of traffic). A problem caught at 1% means 1% of users affected for 5 minutes, not 100% after a quarterly deployment.

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_it_is: GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI/CD platform. **Workflow**: a YAML file in `.github/workflows/` triggered by GitHub events (`push`, `pull_request`, `schedule`, `workflow_dispatch`). **Job**: a unit of work running on a runner (Ubuntu, Windows, macOS). Jobs run in parallel by default; sequential with `needs:`. **Step**: a command (`run:`) or action (`uses:`) within a job. **Action**: reusable unit of logic — can be a JavaScript action, Docker container, or composite action. **Marketplace**: 20,000+ community-built actions (checkout, setup-dotnet, deploy-to-k8s, slack-notify). Runners: GitHub-hosted (free tier: 2000 min/month for public, limited for private) or self-hosted.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.why_it_exists: Before GitHub Actions (2019), teams used separate CI systems (Jenkins, Travis CI, CircleCI) that required external credentials, separate dashboards, and disconnected from pull request workflows. GitHub Actions is native: PRs show inline CI status, secrets are managed in GitHub Settings, and workflows are in the same repo as the code. The marketplace enables composable CI: `uses: actions/setup-node@v4` is one line to set up Node.js, not a custom bash script.
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.how_it_works:
```yaml
# .github/workflows/full-ci-cd.yml
name: CI/CD

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: '0 6 * * MON'  # Weekly nightly full test suite

env:
  REGISTRY: ghcr.io
  IMAGE_NAME: ${{ github.repository }}

jobs:
  # Jobs in same event run in PARALLEL by default
  unit-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '9.x' }

  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '9.x' }
      - run: dotnet format --verify-no-changes

  integration-tests:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: unit-tests  # runs AFTER unit-tests
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:16
        env: { POSTGRES_PASSWORD: test }
        options: --health-cmd pg_isready
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '9.x' }
      - run: dotnet test --filter 'Category=Integration' --configuration Release

  build-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [unit-tests, lint]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'  # only on main branch
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}  # built-in secret
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}

  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [build-push, integration-tests]
    environment: production  # requires approval
    steps:
      - name: Deploy to production
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4  # marketplace action
        with:
          manifests: k8s/
          images: ${{ env.REGISTRY }}/${{ env.IMAGE_NAME }}:${{ github.sha }}
```

15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.use_when: Use GitHub Actions for all CI/CD when code is in GitHub — it's the simplest integration (no external service needed), secrets are managed in GitHub, and PR status checks are native. Use self-hosted runners for: compliance (code can't leave your network), GPU workloads (ML training), very long builds (GitHub-hosted runners have 6h timeout).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.avoid_when: Avoid GitHub Actions for: complex multi-repo orchestration (Jenkins or Argo Workflows are more powerful), when your repo is in GitLab/Bitbucket (use their native CI), and when GitHub Actions minutes cost is prohibitive (consider self-hosted runners or alternative CI for large-scale private repos).
15|🔴 T1 DevOps & Version Control|CI/CD &.what_goes_wrong:
- GITHUB_TOKEN permissions: by default `GITHUB_TOKEN` has read permissions only on fork PRs (to prevent malicious PRs from accessing secrets).
