15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Two strategies for handling increased load. **Vertical scaling (scale up)**: add more resources to the existing machine — more CPU cores, more RAM, faster SSD. Limit: the biggest single machine (AWS: `u-24tb1.metal`, 448 vCPUs, 24TB RAM). Simple: no application changes required. **Horizontal scaling (scale out)**: add more machines running the same application — from 1 server to 10 servers behind a load balancer. Limit: theoretically unlimited, but requires application to be stateless (or externalize state to Redis/database). Horizontal scaling is the cloud-native default — design for it from day one.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Every system has traffic spikes. Vertical scaling has a ceiling (biggest VM is finite) and single point of failure (one machine down = system down). Horizontal scaling enables: cost efficiency (run 1 server at low traffic, auto-scale to 10 during Black Friday), high availability (one server down, others serve requests), and geographic distribution (servers in multiple regions). Cloud auto-scaling (AWS Auto Scaling Groups, Kubernetes HPA) makes horizontal scaling automatic.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.how_it_works:
```
Vertical Scaling:
  t2.micro → t2.xlarge → c5.4xlarge → x2gd.16xlarge
  ($9/mo)    ($150/mo)   ($680/mo)    ($6,000/mo)
  PRO: no application changes, simple
  CON: downtime during resize, single point of failure, cost ceiling

Horizontal Scaling:
  1 server → 3 servers behind ALB → 20 servers (auto-scaled)
  Requirements:
  - Stateless app: no local session state (use Redis/JWT instead)
  - External state: database, cache, message queue (not in-process)
  - Load balancer: distributes requests across instances
  - Health checks: LB removes unhealthy instances
  - Auto-scaling: scale in/out based on CPU, requests/sec

Auto Scaling (AWS example):
  Desired: 3 instances
  Min: 1 instance (cost floor)
  Max: 50 instances (cost ceiling)
  Policy: scale out when CPU > 70% for 2 minutes
          scale in when CPU < 30% for 10 minutes

  Black Friday peak: 3 → 47 instances in 3 minutes
  4am: 47 → 3 instances, cost drops
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use vertical scaling for: databases (stateful, horizontal is complex — use vertical first), single-tenant applications, early startup (simplicity matters), and workloads with memory requirements too high for commodity VMs. Use horizontal scaling for: stateless web/API layers, compute-intensive tasks (ML inference farms), and any system needing high availability or >2× current capacity.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid horizontal scaling without externalising state — if each server has its own cache or in-memory session, requests from the same user to different servers see inconsistent state. Avoid vertical scaling as the primary strategy at scale — it has a price ceiling and SPOF.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Sticky sessions anti-pattern: horizontal scaling with sticky sessions (load balancer always routes user to same server) defeats the purpose — if that server dies, the user loses session. Use JWT tokens (stateless, client-side) or shared session store (Redis) instead.
- Scaling the wrong tier: app servers horizontally scaled to 50 instances, all pointing at one database. The bottleneck moves to the database — connection pool exhausted, database CPU maxed. Horizontal scaling must consider every tier: app servers + caching layer + database replicas (read replicas for horizontal read scaling) + CDN for static assets.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Airbnb during COVID recovery (2021): traffic went from 20% of normal (lockdowns) to 400% of normal (pent-up travel demand) in 8 weeks. Horizontal auto-scaling (AWS EC2 + ALB) allowed Airbnb to go from 20 application servers to 200 automatically. The stateless design (all sessions in Redis, all user data in Aurora MySQL) enabled this. A vertically-scaled monolith on the biggest available VM would have been overwhelmed — the horizontal design made 10× traffic a configuration change, not a re-architecture.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Consistent hashing is an algorithm for distributing data (cache entries, database shards) across nodes such that when a node is added or removed, only 1/n of data needs to be remapped (where n = number of nodes). In regular modulo hashing (`key % n`), adding one node remaps nearly all keys. Consistent hashing places both keys and nodes on a conceptual ring (hash circle 0 to 2^32). A key is assigned to the first node clockwise from its hash position on the ring. Adding a node only steals keys from its immediate clockwise neighbour; removing a node redistributes only its keys to its neighbour.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Cache invalidation is expensive: if you have 3 Memcached servers and you add a 4th using `key % n` hashing, most cache keys now map to different servers — massive cache miss storm, database gets hammered. Consistent hashing minimises cache misses when adding/removing nodes. Used by: Amazon DynamoDB (data partitioning), Apache Cassandra (ring topology), Redis Cluster (hash slots are consistent hashing variant), distributed CDNs.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.how_it_works:
```
Hash ring (0 to 2^32-1, circular):

         0
       /   \
N3 (300)    N1 (100)
     |           |
   N2 (200)      |
       \        /
        --------

Key assignment:
  hash(key) → position on ring → first node clockwise
  hash('order:123') = 150 → first node clockwise from 150 = N2 (200) ✓
  hash('user:456')  = 250 → first node clockwise from 250 = N3 (300) ✓
  hash('prod:789')  = 50  → first node clockwise from 50  = N1 (100) ✓

Adding a node N4 at position 175:
  N4 is clockwise after N2 (200)? No. N4 is between N1 (100) and N2 (200)
  Keys between 100 and 175 that were going to N2 now go to N4
  ONLY keys in (100, 175] range remapped — everything else unchanged

Virtual nodes (vnodes):
  Problem: uneven distribution with few nodes
  Solution: each physical node maps to 150 virtual nodes on the ring
  N1 → positions: 23, 107, 234, 456, 789, ...
  N2 → positions: 45, 189, 312, 567, 901, ...
  Ensures even key distribution and even load redistribution when a node fails

Consistent hashing in Redis Cluster:
  16,384 hash slots (0-16383)
  hash(key) = CRC16(key) % 16384
  Slots distributed across nodes: N1: 0-5460, N2: 5461-10922, N3: 10923-16383
  Adding N4: move slots from existing nodes to N4 (live slot migration)
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use consistent hashing for: distributed caches (Memcached, Redis Cluster), database sharding where you need to add/remove shards, distributed hash tables (DHTs in P2P systems), and any system where the set of nodes changes and remapping keys is expensive (cache invalidation, data migration).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid consistent hashing for small fixed sets of nodes (2-3 servers that never change) — regular modulo hashing is simpler. Avoid if data is accessed by range (consistent hashing doesn't preserve key ordering — use B-tree range partitioning instead).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Hot spots with few nodes: 3 physical nodes on the ring have uneven key distribution by chance. Fix: virtual nodes. Without vnodes, 3 nodes might handle 60%, 30%, 10% of keys respectively. With 150 vnodes per physical node, distribution approaches 33% each.
- Node failure cascade: consistent hashing routes keys for a failed node to the next node clockwise. If that node is already at capacity, it gets overloaded, fails, and its keys cascade to the next — domino failure. Replication (each key stored on k consecutive nodes) and capacity headroom prevent this.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Amazon DynamoDB uses consistent hashing with virtual nodes for its partition key space. When you create a table with partition key `orderId`, DynamoDB maps the key space to its storage nodes using consistent hashing. When DynamoDB adds server capacity (happens automatically), only a fraction of partition key ranges need to migrate — no downtime, minimal cache invalidation. Cassandra's ring topology is explicitly visible: `nodetool ring` shows each token position on the ring and which node owns it.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers (Points of Presence, PoPs) that cache and serve content from locations close to users. When a user in Tokyo requests `img.example.com/logo.png`, instead of fetching from a server in Virginia (200ms), they get it from a CDN edge node in Tokyo (5ms). CDN providers: Cloudflare (200+ PoPs), AWS CloudFront (400+ PoPs), Fastly, Akamai. Content types CDNs serve: static assets (images, JS, CSS), video streaming (HLS/DASH), API responses, and (with edge compute) dynamic content.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Network latency is bounded by the speed of light: Virginia to Tokyo is 170ms round-trip minimum (physics). A page loading 10 resources from Virginia = 10 × 170ms = 1.7 seconds in network alone. A CDN in Tokyo = 10 × 5ms = 50ms. For global users, CDNs are not optional for performance — they're the difference between a usable and unusable product. Additionally, CDNs absorb DDoS attacks (edge nodes absorb attack traffic before it reaches origin), reduce origin server load (cached responses never hit origin), and improve availability (edge nodes serve cached content even if origin is down).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.how_it_works:
```
CDN request flow:

1. User in Tokyo: GET img.example.com/logo.png
2. DNS resolves img.example.com → Cloudflare's nearest Tokyo IP
3. Tokyo edge node checks cache:
   HIT:  Returns cached logo.png → user in 5ms
   MISS: Fetches from origin (Virginia), caches it, returns → user in 205ms
         (subsequent requests from Tokyo: 5ms)

Cache control headers (set by origin):
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable  ← static assets (1 year cache)
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=300                  ← semi-dynamic (5 min cache)
  Cache-Control: private, no-store                    ← user-specific, never cache

CDN configuration:
  - Origin: api.example.com (your servers)
  - Edge locations: Cloudflare's 200+ global PoPs
  - Cache rules:
      /static/*     → cache 1 year (fingerprinted filenames: style.abc123.css)
      /api/products → cache 5 min (stale-while-revalidate)
      /api/user/*   → never cache (dynamic user data)

Edge compute (Cloudflare Workers, Fastly Compute):
  Run JavaScript/Wasm AT the CDN edge → API responses without origin roundtrip
  Use case: A/B testing, personalisation, auth token validation, geolocation
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use CDN for: all public-facing static assets (images, JS bundles, CSS, fonts, videos), API responses that are the same for all users (product catalog, public content), and large file downloads. Mandatory for global applications with users on multiple continents. Use edge compute for: lightweight dynamic responses that need low latency globally (personalised homepage, geolocation-aware routing).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid caching user-specific or sensitive data at CDN edge nodes (private account data, medical records, payment info). Avoid CDN for real-time WebSocket or gRPC streaming (CDNs are for HTTP request/response, not persistent connections — though Cloudflare Spectrum extends CDN to TCP).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Cache poisoning: if a CDN caches a response containing user-specific data (user ID in the response, API returned `Cache-Control: public` incorrectly), it serves another user's data to everyone. Always set `Cache-Control: private` for user-specific responses and `Vary: Cookie, Authorization` when responses differ per user.
- Cache invalidation delay: a CDN edge node may serve stale content for up to `max-age` seconds after origin is updated. For urgent updates (critical bug fix, wrong price), use CDN cache purge API (`cloudflare.com API: POST /zones/{zone}/purge_cache`). Use content-fingerprinted filenames (`style.abc123.css`) for static assets — changing the file changes the URL, no cache invalidation needed.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Twitch (livestreaming CDN at scale): a popular streamer with 100,000 concurrent viewers. Without CDN: 100,000 viewers fetching video segments from one origin server = origin dies. With CDN: each CDN PoP serves a local cluster of viewers. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Rate limiting controls the number of requests a client can make in a time window. Four main algorithms: **Fixed Window Counter**: count requests in fixed time buckets (100 requests per minute — reset counter at :00, :01, etc.). **Sliding Window Log**: record timestamp of each request, count requests in the last 60 seconds (accurate but memory intensive). **Sliding Window Counter**: hybrid — uses two fixed windows weighted by time elapsed (memory efficient, nearly as accurate as sliding log). **Token Bucket**: tokens added at rate r, each request consumes one token, bucket capacity = burst limit (allows bursts up to capacity). **Leaky Bucket**: requests queue; processed at fixed rate (smooth output regardless of burst).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Without rate limiting: one misbehaving client (DDoS, runaway script, billing bug) can consume all server resources and deny service to all others. Rate limiting protects: API availability (fair usage among clients), cost control (prevent expensive accidental over-usage), security (brute-force login prevention), and business model enforcement (free tier: 100 requests/day, paid: 10,000/day).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Implement rate limiting for: all public APIs (prevent abuse), authentication endpoints (brute-force prevention — aggressive limits: 5 attempts per minute per IP), webhooks/callbacks (prevent callback storms), and LLM API calls (expensive per-request, easy to accidentally over-call). Use Redis for distributed rate limiting (state shared across all API servers).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid rate limiting for: internal service-to-service calls where you control both sides (use circuit breakers instead), trusted internal admin APIs, and batch processing endpoints designed for high-volume (implement quota-based limits instead of per-second rate limits for batch).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- IP-based rate limiting with NAT: an office of 200 employees behind a single NAT IP address all share one rate limit — one rogue employee's script blocks everyone. Use user-ID based rate limiting where authentication is available; fall back to IP only for unauthenticated endpoints.
- Race conditions in distributed rate limiting without Redis transactions: two API servers both check Redis (token = 1), both see 'allow', both decrement to 0 — now token count is -1, two requests were allowed instead of one. Fix: Redis Lua scripts (atomic check-and-decrement) or Redis transactions with WATCH.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: GitHub API rate limiting: authenticated: 5,000 requests/hour per user (token bucket, hourly capacity). Unauthenticated: 60 requests/hour per IP (prevents scraping). Response headers: `X-RateLimit-Limit: 5000`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining: 4237`, `X-RateLimit-Reset: 1718000000` (Unix timestamp when limit resets). Tools like Terraform's GitHub provider respect these headers, backing off automatically when `X-RateLimit-Remaining < 100`. The reset timestamp enables clients to sleep until the window resets rather than busy-polling.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures in distributed systems by detecting when a downstream service is failing and stopping calls to it temporarily, instead of timing out on every request. Three states: **Closed** (normal — requests pass through, failures tracked). **Open** (tripped — requests fail immediately without calling downstream, returns cached or error response). **Half-Open** (recovery probe — after timeout, allows a limited number of test requests; if they succeed, closes; if they fail, opens again). Named after electrical circuit breakers: when too much current flows, the breaker opens to prevent damage.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Without circuit breakers: when the payment service is down, every checkout request waits for the 30-second HTTP timeout before failing. 1000 concurrent checkouts × 30 seconds = 30,000 thread-seconds of waiting, thread pool exhaustion, then the checkout service crashes too. The payment service's failure cascades to the checkout service, then to the API gateway, then everything is down. Circuit breaker breaks this chain: 'payment service is down, fail immediately with a 503, don't wait'.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use circuit breakers for: all synchronous cross-service HTTP calls, database connection pools (circuit breaks on connection pool exhaustion), external API calls (third-party payment processors, SMS gateways, email services). Every call that can block your thread should have a circuit breaker. In .NET: Polly. In Java: Resilience4j. In service mesh: Istio handles circuit breaking in the sidecar (no code change needed).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid circuit breakers for: internal method calls (no network — circuit breaker adds overhead without benefit), very short-lived operations where timeout is sufficient, and idempotent operations where retry is the correct failure strategy (use retry instead of circuit break for DNS resolution).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Circuit breaker too sensitive: `SamplingDuration = 5s, FailureRatio = 0.3, MinimumThroughput = 3` — 3 failures in 5 seconds opens the circuit. A brief network blip trips the breaker for 15 seconds, serving errors to users when the service recovered in 2 seconds. Tune for your SLA: sample window should be long enough to distinguish a blip from an outage.
- All-or-nothing failure: circuit open means ALL requests fail. For degraded (not failed) downstreams, prefer fallback patterns: return cached data, return a reduced feature set, or return a 'service temporarily unavailable' message with a Retry-After header rather than a generic 500.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Netflix Hystrix (now replaced by Resilience4j): Netflix's streaming service calls 30+ microservices per page load. Hystrix wraps every inter-service call. When the Recommendation service goes down: Hystrix opens its circuit, returns a default 'Popular Movies' list (fallback) instead of an error. Users see slightly less personalised content; they can still watch Netflix. Without circuit breakers: Recommendation service failure would cascade to the home page service, making Netflix's home page error for all users.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: The Saga pattern manages distributed transactions across multiple microservices where a single ACID transaction is impossible (services have separate databases). A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event or message to trigger the next step. If any step fails, compensating transactions roll back the previous steps. Two implementations: **Choreography** — each service listens for events and reacts (decentralised, no central coordinator). **Orchestration** — a central Saga Orchestrator sends commands to each service in sequence (centralised, explicit flow control). Example: place order → debit inventory → charge payment → ship. If payment fails → refund inventory → cancel order.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: In a monolith: `BEGIN TRANSACTION; update inventory; charge payment; create shipment; COMMIT` — all or nothing. In microservices: each service has its own database, no cross-database transactions. Without sagas: you charge payment, then inventory service crashes — you've taken money without reserving stock. Sagas provide 'eventual consistency with compensation': instead of ACID atomicity, you get ACD (Atomicity, Consistency, Durability) through compensating transactions.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use sagas for: distributed business workflows spanning multiple services (order fulfilment, user onboarding, booking systems), any workflow that requires all-or-nothing semantics across multiple microservice databases, and long-running processes (saga state persisted durably, can resume after a service restart).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid sagas when: a single service with one database can own the entire workflow (use ACID transactions instead), when compensating transactions are impossible ('unsubscribe from email' can be compensated; 'launch rocket' cannot), and when the team doesn't have the observability to trace saga execution across services (distributed tracing is mandatory for debugging sagas).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Saga rollback is not atomic: between the failure and the compensating transaction executing, the system is in an inconsistent state (stock reserved, payment declined, refund not yet processed). During this window, the item appears 'reserved' to other customers. Design for: idempotent compensating transactions, timeouts on pending saga steps, and monitoring for sagas stuck in intermediate states.
- Choreography observability: a choreography saga (events, no central coordinator) is hard to trace. 'Why was this order never fulfilled?' requires tracing events across 5 services' logs. Use correlation IDs on every event and OpenTelemetry distributed tracing to reconstruct saga execution timelines.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Uber's trip booking: saga coordinates driver assignment, payment preauthorisation, and ETA calculation across separate services. If driver assignment succeeds but payment preauthorisation fails (card declined), a compensating transaction releases the driver (unassigns them from the trip) and notifies the rider. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: The Bulkhead pattern isolates critical resources into separate pools so that failures in one pool don't exhaust resources needed by others — named after ship bulkheads that partition a hull into watertight compartments (one compartment floods, ship stays afloat). 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Shared resource exhaustion cascades: if all services share a 100-thread pool, and the recommendation service (slow ML calls) occupies 95 threads waiting on slow responses, there are only 5 threads left for all other requests including time-critical payment processing. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use bulkheads for: isolating critical-path services (payments, auth) from non-critical services (recommendations, analytics), separating client-facing traffic from internal background processing, and any scenario where one slow downstream service could exhaust all system resources. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Back-pressure is a mechanism for a downstream component (consumer) to signal to an upstream component (producer) that it's receiving data faster than it can process it — 'slow down.' Without back-pressure: the producer keeps sending, the consumer's buffer fills up, and either data is dropped or memory is exhausted. With back-pressure: the producer adapts its rate to match the consumer's processing capacity. Implemented in: Reactive Streams spec (RxJava, Project Reactor, Akka Streams), .NET `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` (implicitly via async iteration), gRPC streaming, Kafka consumer lag monitoring.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: A producer-consumer mismatch is common: an IoT device sends 10,000 sensor readings/second; the processing pipeline can handle 1,000/second. Without back-pressure: 9,000/second fill up buffers, memory exhausts, JVM OOM crash. With back-pressure: the pipeline signals 'I can handle 1,000/second', the producer throttles or the excess is handled gracefully (dropped with metrics, or stored for later processing). Back-pressure is essential for resilient streaming pipelines.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Apply back-pressure for: real-time data streaming (IoT, log ingestion, event streams), video/audio streaming pipelines, database query result streaming (`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` from EF Core), and any producer-consumer pipeline where production rate can exceed consumption rate. `Channel<T>` with `BoundedChannelOptions` is the .NET idiom; Kafka consumer groups provide natural back-pressure for distributed streaming.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid back-pressure for: request-response APIs (back-pressure semantics are built-in via HTTP — slow server means slow response), in-memory computations where both producer and consumer run at the same speed, and when dropping data is acceptable (lossy streaming with latest-value-only semantics — use `DropOldest` or `DropNewest` channel modes).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: .NET's `HttpClient` when downloading large files: `await response.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync()` → `await stream.ReadAsync(buffer, ...)`. When you `await ReadAsync()`, you're participating in a back-pressure chain from your code all the way to the server's network interface.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: A service mesh is a dedicated infrastructure layer for handling service-to-service communication in a microservices architecture — adding features like mTLS (mutual TLS), circuit breaking, retries, load balancing, distributed tracing, and traffic management without changing application code. Implemented as sidecar proxies: each service pod gets an injected sidecar container (Envoy proxy for Istio, Cilium for eBPF-based meshes) that intercepts all inbound/outbound traffic. Popular service meshes: **Istio** (Envoy sidecar, full-featured), **Linkerd** (Rust sidecar, lightweight), **Cilium** (eBPF-based, no sidecar overhead). Control plane: configures all sidecars centrally.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: In a microservices architecture with 50 services, each service needs: retry logic, circuit breaking, timeout configuration, mTLS (encrypt all inter-service traffic), and distributed tracing — implemented consistently. Without a service mesh: each team implements this differently in their service (Polly for .NET, Resilience4j for Java, custom Go middleware). With a service mesh: the infrastructure handles it consistently for all services, regardless of language. Operations teams configure retry/circuit breaking policies centrally; developers don't need to know the details.

```yaml
# Istio traffic management (VirtualService)
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  http:
  - match:
    - headers: { x-api-version: { exact: v2 } }
    route:
    - destination: { host: payment-service, subset: v2 }  # header-based routing

  - route:
    - destination: { host: payment-service, subset: v1 }  # default: v1
      weight: 90
    - destination: { host: payment-service, subset: v2 }  # canary: v2
      weight: 10
    retries:
      attempts: 3
      perTryTimeout: 2s
    timeout: 10s

---
# DestinationRule: circuit breaking
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: payment-service
spec:
  host: payment-service
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http: { http1MaxPendingRequests: 100 }
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5          # open circuit after 5 consecutive 5xx
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s            # eject for 30 seconds
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels: { version: v1 }
  - name: v2
    labels: { version: v2 }

# mTLS: all inter-service communication encrypted automatically
# No code change needed in payment-service or calling services
# Istio sidecar proxies handle certificate rotation, TLS handshake
```

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid service meshes for: small microservice deployments (<5 services), monoliths, and teams without Kubernetes expertise (service meshes require significant ops knowledge). The sidecar proxy adds 1-5ms latency per hop and 2-5% memory overhead per pod. Cilium's eBPF approach eliminates sidecar overhead but requires kernel 4.9+.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- mTLS certificate bootstrap deadlock: Istio requires mutual TLS between services including the istiod control plane. During initial cluster setup, pods can get stuck waiting for certificates that require pods to already be running. Use `PERMISSIVE` mTLS mode during bootstrap, then switch to `STRICT`.
- Traffic management config complexity: Istio's VirtualService + DestinationRule + Gateway + ServiceEntry configuration becomes complex for 50+ services. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Distributed tracing tracks a single user request as it flows through multiple microservices, recording timing, errors, and metadata at each hop. Each request gets a unique **trace ID** propagated through all services via HTTP headers (`traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01`). Each service creates **spans** — child spans nested under the root span. A trace visualised shows: 'Order request: 245ms total — 5ms API gateway, 12ms auth service, 178ms database query, 50ms payment service'. Tools: OpenTelemetry (standard instrumentation), Jaeger, Zipkin, Tempo, AWS X-Ray, Honeycomb.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: In microservices, 'why is this request slow?' can't be answered by looking at one service's logs. A 2-second user request may touch 10 services; the latency could be in any of them. Without distributed tracing: correlate logs across 10 services by timestamp and request ID (manual, error-prone). With distributed tracing: one trace view shows the waterfall of spans, immediately identifying the slow hop (the `inventory-service.FindAvailableStock` span took 1.8 seconds — that's the bottleneck).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Implement distributed tracing for: all microservice architectures (mandatory for effective debugging), serverless functions (trace across Lambda invocations), and any system where a request touches more than 2 services. Use OpenTelemetry as the standard SDK — it's provider-agnostic, supported by all major APM tools (Jaeger, Zipkin, Honeycomb, Datadog, New Relic, AWS X-Ray).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid implementing custom tracing (inventing your own trace ID propagation, custom log correlation) — use OpenTelemetry, which is the CNCF standard. Avoid sampling 100% of traces in high-throughput production (excessive overhead and storage cost) — sample 1-10% of requests, 100% of errors.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Missing context propagation: a service that makes HTTP calls without propagating the `traceparent` header breaks the trace chain. Downstream services start new traces — you see fragments, not the complete request. Use `HttpClientInstrumentation` (OpenTelemetry) which propagates automatically for all `HttpClient` calls.
- Trace sampling bias: sampling 1% of requests misses rare errors (error rate 0.1% — you'd need 10x the sample rate to see them). Use tail-based sampling (Jaeger supports this via Tempo/OpenTelemetry Collector): sample 1% of successful requests, 100% of failed/slow requests. Captures the important traces without overhead.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Shopify's order processing: a `POST /checkout` request touches 12 services (inventory, customer, pricing, tax, payment, fraud, order, notification, analytics, logging, warehouse, shipping). OpenTelemetry traces flow through all 12 services with one trace ID. When the Black Friday P99 latency spiked to 3.2 seconds (from 800ms normally), tracing showed the tax-calculation service's `TaxJar API` call was taking 2.1 seconds. Without tracing: hours of log correlation across 12 service logs to find the bottleneck. With tracing: identified in 2 minutes from the Jaeger waterfall view.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Chaos engineering is the discipline of deliberately introducing failures into production (or production-like) systems to discover weaknesses before they cause unplanned outages. Netflix coined the term (2011) with Chaos Monkey — a tool that randomly terminates EC2 instances during business hours. The principle: if failures will happen (servers die, networks partition, dependencies go down), you'd rather discover the failure mode and your system's response during a controlled experiment than at 3am during peak traffic. Key tools: Chaos Monkey, Chaos Mesh (Kubernetes), Gremlin, LitmusChaos, AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Distributed systems fail in unexpected ways: circuit breakers that were never triggered in testing may not work as configured in production. Graceful degradation code paths may have bugs that only manifest under real failure conditions. Chaos engineering surfaces these weaknesses proactively. Netflix runs Chaos Monkey in production continuously — if any service can't survive random instance termination, the team finds out during business hours (engineers available to fix it) not during Friday night peak traffic.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.how_it_works:
```
Chaos Engineering process (Principles of Chaos Engineering, Netflix 2016):

1. Define steady state: what does 'normal' look like?
   Metrics: 99.9% checkout success, P99 latency < 500ms, error rate < 0.1%

2. Hypothesize: 'Killing one payment-service pod will not affect checkout success rate
   because we have 3 pods and the load balancer detects unhealthy pods in <10s'

3. Introduce failure (blast radius controlled):
   - Start small: one pod, not all pods
   - Monitor closely
   - Define abort criteria: if checkout success drops below 95%, stop experiment

4. Measure actual vs steady state:
   - Actual: checkout success drops to 97% for 12 seconds during pod restart
   - Hypothesis confirmed (still above 99%)

5. Fix weaknesses discovered, then increase blast radius

Chaos types (Chaos Mesh for Kubernetes):
  - Pod failure: kill pods, nodes
  - Network chaos: inject latency (50ms), packet loss (10%), partition services
  - CPU/Memory stress: consume 80% CPU, exhaust memory
  - Time chaos: skew system clock (breaks JWT expiry, cache TTLs)
  - IO chaos: inject disk latency, fill disk

Example (AWS FIS):
  aws fis create-experiment-template \n    --targets '{"paymentPods": {"resourceType": "aws:eks:pod", "selectionMode": "PERCENT(20)"}}' \n    --actions '{"kill20pct": {"actionId": "aws:eks:terminate-pod-by-selector", "targets": {"Pods": "paymentPods"}}}' \n    --stop-conditions '[{"source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm", "value": "PaymentErrorRate>5pct"}]'
  # Kills 20% of payment pods, stops automatically if error rate exceeds 5%
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Use chaos engineering when: your system has circuit breakers, retry logic, and failover mechanisms that have never been tested under real failure conditions, when you're meeting SLAs (chaos proves the SLA is real, not theoretical), before major events (Black Friday chaos runs 4 weeks before), and for compliance (some regulations require demonstrated resilience).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Never run chaos experiments on production without mature observability (you need to see the impact), on systems without sufficient redundancy (chaos on a single-instance database = data loss), or without a rollback plan. Start in staging/lower environments, build confidence, then graduate to production with very controlled blast radius.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- Underestimating blast radius: 'kill one pod' in a 3-pod deployment is 33% capacity reduction, not 'just one pod down.' If pods are sized for 50% capacity each (common misconfig), 33% capacity reduction creates a cascading overload on the remaining pods.
- Chaos without observability: running chaos experiments without real-time dashboards is flying blind. You need metrics showing the impact in real-time to know when to abort. Chaos engineering requires mature observability as a prerequisite.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Netflix Simian Army (2011-2019): Chaos Monkey (random instance termination), Chaos Gorilla (terminate entire Availability Zone), Chaos Kong (terminate entire AWS Region). Netflix runs Chaos Monkey continuously during business hours. Any service that crashes when an instance is terminated requires the owning team to fix it. Result: Netflix engineers never wake up to an 'instance died' alert — their systems handle instance termination automatically because they've been tested continuously under chaos conditions for a decade.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_it_is: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is Google's approach to applying software engineering to operations problems — treating operations (reliability, scaling, incident response) as software engineering problems rather than manual IT processes. Core concepts: **SLI** (Service Level Indicator — a metric: 'fraction of requests succeeding in <500ms'). **SLO** (Service Level Objective — target: 'SLI ≥ 99.9%'). **SLA** (Service Level Agreement — customer contract: 'we promise 99.9% availability'). **Error budget** (allowed downtime: 99.9% SLO = 8.7 hours downtime/year. Error budget = 8.7h. If you've used 7h, you have 1.7h left. Error budget governs: is it safe to deploy risky changes?)
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.why_it_exists: Traditional ops ('sysadmins') maintained systems manually — every change was a manual step, scaling required provisioning physical servers, incidents were heroic overnight efforts. SRE (Ben Treynor Sloss, Google 2003) treated reliability as an engineering problem: automate operations, measure reliability with SLIs, balance feature velocity against reliability through error budgets. The key insight: 100% reliability is impossible and not desirable (it prevents all change). The error budget creates a mathematically-derived risk tolerance for deployments.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.how_it_works:
```
SRE framework:

1. Define SLIs:
   - Availability SLI: (successful requests) / (total requests)
   - Latency SLI: fraction of requests completing in < 200ms
   - Error SLI: fraction of requests with no server-side errors

2. Set SLOs:
   - Availability SLO: 99.9% (over rolling 30 days)
   - Latency SLO: 95% of requests < 200ms
   - Error SLO: 99.95% success rate

3. Calculate error budget:
   99.9% availability → 0.1% failure allowed
   30 days × 0.1% = 43.2 minutes/month of allowed downtime
   At 1000 req/sec: 43,200 seconds of failure seconds allowed (43.2 min at all requests failing)

4. Error budget governance:
   Budget consumed = (1 - actual_availability) × duration
   Current budget remaining: 20 minutes (depleted 23 of 43 minutes this month)
   → Engineering decision: is this week's risky database migration worth 20 minutes of budget?
   → If yes: deploy with rollback plan, cancel if budget hits 0
   → If budget is 0: no risky changes until next month resets budget

5. SRE toil reduction:
   Toil = repetitive, manual, tactical work (acknowledging same alert 30× a week)
   SRE target: < 50% time on toil. > 50% → automate the toil

   Toil examples:
   - Manual alert acknowledgment → auto-remediation runbooks
   - Manual capacity planning → predictive auto-scaling
   - Manual incident reports → automated postmortems from trace data

Incident management:
   Severity 1 (P1): >1% of users affected, on-call paged, 15-min response SLA
   Severity 2 (P2): degraded performance, 1-hour response SLA
   Post-incident review: blameless, within 5 business days
   Action items tracked in backlog, closed within 30 days
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.use_when: Apply SRE for: production services with formal SLAs, services where downtime has financial impact, large engineering organizations where ops/dev coordination is complex. Even without full SRE implementation, define SLIs and SLOs for every customer-facing service — they make the implicit ('we should be reliable') explicit ('we promise 99.9% and here's how we measure it').
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.avoid_when: Avoid SRE practices for: internal dev tools, batch jobs without latency requirements, prototypes/MVPs. Over-engineering SRE practices for a 2-person startup adds process overhead without proportionate benefit. Scale SRE practice to team and customer maturity.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.what_goes_wrong:
- SLOs without consequences: define 99.9% SLO, breach it consistently, and take no action. SLOs without error budget governance are decorative. Error budgets must be enforced: when exhausted, deploy freezes until budget resets. This requires buy-in from product and leadership — SRE is an organizational practice, not just a technical one.
- Measuring the wrong SLI: measuring server-side error rate (0.01%) while users experience 5% frontend errors (CORS issues, CDN misconfigurations, client-side timeouts). SLIs must measure from the user's perspective (synthetic monitoring, client-side RUM — Real User Monitoring). Server metrics alone miss user-experience failures.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sys.real_example: Google's public SRE book (2016): G Suite's 99.99% availability SLO (52 minutes downtime/year allowed). Google SREs use error budgets to decide when to deploy risky changes to Google Drive. If the error budget is depleted for the quarter, the Drive team can't deploy new features — they must spend the remaining quarter improving reliability until the budget resets. This creates a mathematical relationship between feature velocity and reliability that both engineering and business can reason about.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.what_it_is: SAST (Static Application Security Testing) analyses source code, bytecode, or binary without executing it to find security vulnerabilities. Tools inspect code patterns against a vulnerability database: SQL injection (`string.Format("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id={0}", userId)` — direct string concatenation), hardcoded credentials (`password = "admin123"`), insecure cryptography (`MD5.Create()`), path traversal, XSS patterns. Tools: SonarQube, Checkmarx, Semgrep, GitHub CodeQL, Snyk Code, Bandit (Python). SAST runs in CI/CD (shift-left) — catches vulnerabilities before code reaches production.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.why_it_exists: Security code review by humans is expensive, inconsistent, and doesn't scale. SAST automates the pattern recognition: 'does any code in this 50,000-line PR use string concatenation in SQL queries?' A human reviewer might miss one occurrence; SAST scans every line. SAST is the first layer of the security testing stack: fast (minutes, not days), runs automatically in CI, gives developers immediate feedback on security issues in their own code.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.how_it_works:
```yaml
# GitHub CodeQL in GitHub Actions
name: Security Scan

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  codeql:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v3
        with:
          languages: 'csharp,javascript'
          queries: security-extended  # includes OWASP Top 10

      - uses: actions/setup-dotnet@v4
        with: { dotnet-version: '9.x' }
      - run: dotnet build

      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v3
        with:
          category: /language:csharp

# Semgrep for custom rules:
# semgrep --config=p/owasp-top-ten --config=p/csharp .

# Common SAST findings:
# SQL Injection:
#   VULNERABLE:  db.Query($"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='{name}'")  ← SAST flags this
#   SAFE:        db.Query("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name=@name", new { name })

# Hardcoded secret:
#   VULNERABLE:  var apiKey = "sk-abc123..."  ← SAST flags literal that looks like API key
#   SAFE:        var apiKey = configuration["ExternalService:ApiKey"]

# Insecure deserialization:
#   VULNERABLE:  JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(userInput, settings)
#   SAFE:        JsonSerializer.Deserialize<SafeDto>(userInput)  ← typed deserialization

# Path traversal:
#   VULNERABLE:  File.ReadAllText(userProvidedPath)
#   SAFE:        File.ReadAllText(Path.Combine(allowedBaseDir, Path.GetFileName(userProvidedPath)))
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.use_when: Run SAST in CI on every PR for: any web application, API, or service handling user input; authentication code; anything processing financial, health, or PII data. Set SAST as a required CI check — PRs can't merge if SAST reports critical/high severity findings. Use SAST in IDE plugins (SonarLint, Snyk IDE) for real-time feedback while coding.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.avoid_when: Don't rely on SAST alone — it has high false-positive rates (may flag safe code as vulnerable) and misses runtime-only vulnerabilities (authentication bypass via logic flaws, privilege escalation in complex permission systems). SAST is one layer; combine with DAST, penetration testing, and code review.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.what_goes_wrong:
- Alert fatigue from false positives: SAST tools report 200+ findings, 180 of which are false positives. Developers learn to ignore SAST reports. Fix: tune SAST rules for your codebase (suppress known false positives with inline comments), focus on high-confidence, high-severity rules first, and fix issues over time using 'new findings only' mode for PRs.
- SAST bypass via obfuscation: attackers who have code access can craft SQL injection through string manipulation that SAST doesn't detect (`"SELECT" + " * FROM " + table` assembled at runtime). SAST is not a substitute for parameterised queries — it's a safety net to catch slip-ups.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Sof.real_example: Microsoft's Security Development Lifecycle (SDL): every pull request to Azure SDK repositories runs CodeQL. Finding categories: SQL injection, XSS, XXE, insecure random, hardcoded credentials, path traversal. CodeQL has native understanding of .NET's System.Data.SqlClient — it traces data from user input through string formatting to SQL execution and flags the path. When a developer writes `new SqlCommand($"SELECT * FROM {userTable}")`, CodeQL traces `userTable` to user input and flags: 'SQL injection vulnerability — user-controlled data in SQL query construction.'

A01: Broken Access Control
  Example: GET /api/orders/123 (your order)

  Fix: bcrypt, scrypt, Argon2 (slow hash functions)
  Example: HTTP instead of HTTPS for login page

  Example: no rate limiting on login → brute force 1M passwords in 1 hour
  Example: JWT secret is 'secret' → any attacker can forge tokens
  Fix: bcrypt + rate limiting + account lockout + strong JWT secrets (256-bit random)

  Server fetches AWS metadata → leaks IAM role credentials
  Fix: allowlist external URLs; block private IP ranges (10.x, 172.16.x, 169.254.x)

A05: Security Misconfiguration
  Example: /api/debug endpoint exposed in production
  Example: default credentials (admin/admin) on management console
  Example: Stack traces returned to users (leaks technology stack, file paths)

Zero Trust implementation layers:

1. Identity verification (every request):
   - Users: MFA required, short-lived sessions (1 hour), re-auth on sensitive actions
   - Services: mTLS (mutual TLS) — services authenticate with certificates, not IPs

   spec:
     podSelector:
       matchLabels: { app: order-service }
     ingress:
     - from:

     egress:
     - to:
       - podSelector: { matchLabels: { app: postgres } }     # order-service can only reach postgres

4. Service-to-service mTLS (via Istio):
   Every inter-service call authenticated with X.509 certificates
   Certificate: 'I am order-service, my SPIFFE ID is spiffe://cluster.local/ns/default/sa/order-service'
   Payment-service: 'I accept calls from order-service's SPIFFE ID only'

The 2022 OSSF/Harvard report found that 77% of the world's code is open source — Scorecard helps identify the security quality of those dependencies. Also used internally: enterprises run Scorecard on their own repositories to measure security practices.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: GitOps is an operational model where Git is the single source of truth for both application code AND infrastructure configuration. The desired state of the entire system — Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts, infrastructure-as-code — is stored in a Git repository. A GitOps operator (Argo CD, Flux CD) continuously reconciles actual cluster state with the desired state in Git. To change any configuration: open a PR → merge → operator detects change → applies to cluster. Key principle: every cluster change must be in Git (no `kubectl apply` directly to production).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.why_it_exists: Traditional operational model: someone SSH'd into a production server and ran commands — undocumented, unreviewed, unrevertable. 'Infrastructure drift': production state diverges from what's in code because of ad-hoc changes. GitOps solves: auditability ('who changed what, when' — from git history), reviewability (every change is a PR), revertability (roll back is `git revert` → operator applies), consistency (no drift — operator continuously corrects deviations), and disaster recovery (re-create entire cluster by pointing new cluster at the same Git repo).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.how_it_works:
```
GitOps repositories:
  app-repo/          ← application code (developer commits)
  infra-repo/        ← infrastructure desired state (DevOps commits)
    apps/
      production/
        order-service.yaml    ← Kubernetes Deployment, Service, etc.
        payment-service.yaml
      staging/
        order-service.yaml    ← same charts, different values
    infrastructure/
      networking.yaml         ← VPC, subnets (via Crossplane)
      databases.yaml          ← RDS instances (via Crossplane)

GitOps workflow:
1. Developer: git push changes to app-repo
2. CI pipeline: build + test → push Docker image to registry
   image tag: myapp:abc123-sha
3. CD pipeline: update infra-repo/apps/production/order-service.yaml
   image: myapp:abc123-sha  ← automated PR or direct commit
4. Argo CD (watching infra-repo): detects image tag change
5. Argo CD: applies updated Deployment to Kubernetes cluster
6. Cluster state now matches Git state ← reconciliation complete

Rollback:
  git revert <bad-commit-sha> → Argo CD applies previous Deployment
  No manual kubectl, no ssh — pure Git operations

Drift detection:
  Someone manually patches a Deployment in production (kubectl edit):
  Argo CD detects: 'actual state ≠ Git state'
  Options: auto-correct (self-healing) or alert for manual review
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.use_when: Use GitOps for: all Kubernetes-based production environments (Argo CD or Flux are now industry standard), multi-environment deployments (dev/staging/prod managed from one Git repo with environment-specific values), regulated environments (SOC 2, ISO 27001 — Git history provides the change audit trail), and any team that has experienced infrastructure drift or undocumented changes.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.avoid_when: Avoid GitOps for: non-Kubernetes environments without GitOps operators (classic VM-based infrastructure is better managed with Ansible/Terraform + pipelines), very small teams where the Git PR overhead exceeds the benefit, and secret management (secrets should NOT be in Git — use External Secrets Operator to pull from Vault/AWS Secrets Manager).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_goes_wrong:
- Secrets in Git: storing Kubernetes secrets in the GitOps repo leaks them (even private repos get cloned). Use Sealed Secrets (Bitnami — encrypts secrets in Git, only the cluster can decrypt) or External Secrets Operator (pulls from Vault/AWS SM) to keep secrets out of Git.
- Divergent Git branches: separate branches for each environment with manual merging between them leads to drift between staging and production configs. Prefer a single branch with environment-specific values via Helm/Kustomize overlays — same chart deployed with different values files.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.real_example: Weaveworks (GitOps originators): their internal Kubernetes platform is managed entirely via Git. When a service's resource limits need increasing, an engineer opens a PR modifying the Deployment YAML. PR is reviewed, merged, and Flux CD applies the change within 5 minutes. Rollbacks are `git revert` commands, not emergency `kubectl` sessions.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: Argo CD is a declarative, GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes. It continuously watches a Git repository and automatically syncs the cluster's desired state (defined in Git) with the actual state. Core concepts: **Application** (defines: Git repo URL + path to manifests + target cluster + namespace), **Sync** (reconcile actual cluster state with Git state), **Health status** (Healthy, Progressing, Degraded, Missing), **Rollback** (revert to any previous Git revision), **App of Apps** / **ApplicationSets** (manage 100+ applications). Web UI shows diff between Git state and live cluster state per resource.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.why_it_exists: Traditional CI/CD pushes to Kubernetes: `kubectl apply -f k8s/` baked into a CI pipeline. Problems: CI runner needs cluster access (security risk), no drift detection (direct kubectl applies bypass pipeline), no unified view of all application states, and rollback requires re-running old pipeline. Argo CD is a pull-based operator inside the cluster — the cluster pulls from Git, not the other way around. This is more secure (CI runner doesn't need cluster credentials) and provides a unified deployment dashboard.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.how_it_works:
```yaml
# Argo CD Application manifest
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: order-service
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: 'https://github.com/myorg/infra-repo'
    path: apps/production/order-service  # Helm chart or kustomize directory
    targetRevision: HEAD
    helm:
      valueFiles:
        - values-production.yaml
  destination:
    server: 'https://kubernetes.default.svc'
    namespace: production
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true      # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true   # auto-correct drift (someone manually changes a resource)
    syncOptions:
      - CreateNamespace=true

---
# ApplicationSet: deploy same app to multiple clusters
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: order-service-all-clusters
spec:
  generators:
  - list:
      elements:
      - cluster: eu-west-1
        values: { environment: production, region: eu-west-1 }
      - cluster: us-east-1
        values: { environment: production, region: us-east-1 }
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'order-service-{{cluster}}'
    spec:
      source:
        path: apps/order-service
        helm:
          parameters:
          - name: region
            value: '{{values.region}}'
      destination:
        server: '{{cluster}}'
```

```bash
# Argo CD CLI
argocd app list                           # list all applications
argocd app get order-service              # details + sync status
argocd app sync order-service             # manual sync
argocd app rollback order-service 3       # rollback to revision 3
argocd app diff order-service             # diff Git vs cluster
```

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.avoid_when: Avoid Argo CD for non-Kubernetes environments (it's Kubernetes-native). Avoid for very simple deployments where a `kubectl apply` in CI is sufficient — Argo CD has significant operational overhead (it's a complex multi-component system itself). Consider Flux CD as a lightweight alternative.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_goes_wrong:
- App of Apps bootstrap chicken-and-egg: Argo CD needs to exist to deploy the `app-of-apps` Application that deploys Argo CD. Solution: use `argocd app create` CLI to bootstrap the first App of Apps, then everything else is managed by Argo CD.

Default: all authenticated users are read-only. Explicitly define `argocd-rbac-cm` policies for role-based access (developers: sync only, platform team: admin).

During tax season, they can promote a hotfix from staging to production in 2 minutes: merge the infra-repo PR → Argo CD detects change → syncs all 4000 application instances across 150 clusters within 5 minutes. Pre-Argo CD: rolling update across 150 clusters required coordinated manual work across teams. Post-Argo CD: automated by the platform, triggered by a Git merge.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: Flux CD is a CNCF-graduated GitOps continuous delivery tool for Kubernetes, competing with Argo CD. Flux takes a different architecture: instead of one monolithic server, it's a set of composable controllers: **source-controller** (watches Git repos, Helm repos, OCI registries), **kustomize-controller** (applies Kustomize/raw manifests), **helm-controller** (manages HelmRelease resources), **notification-controller** (sends events to Slack, Teams, Webhook), **image-automation-controller** (updates Git when new Docker images are available). Flux runs as Kubernetes controllers (CRDs), not a separate server.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.why_it_exists: Flux and Argo CD are the two dominant GitOps tools — both solve the same problem differently. Flux is more modular (use only what you need), Kubernetes-native (no separate Flux UI, integrated with kubectl and standard tools), and slightly simpler operationally. Argo CD has a richer UI and more features. Many organisations run both: Flux for application delivery (lightweight), Argo CD for visibility (dashboard). Flux's image automation (detect new Docker image → update Git → trigger sync) is particularly useful for automating image tag updates.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.how_it_works:
```yaml
# Flux bootstraps itself and watches a Git repo
# flux bootstrap github --owner=myorg --repository=infra-repo --branch=main

# GitRepository source (what to watch):
apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: GitRepository
metadata:
  name: infra-repo
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m  # check Git every minute
  url: ssh://git@github.com/myorg/infra-repo
  secretRef:
    name: flux-git-deploy-key
  ref:
    branch: main

---
# Kustomization (what to apply from the Git repo):
apiVersion: kustomize.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Kustomization
metadata:
  name: apps
  namespace: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 10m
  retryInterval: 2m
  sourceRef:
    kind: GitRepository
    name: infra-repo
  path: ./apps/production
  prune: true
  wait: true
  timeout: 5m

---
# HelmRelease (deploy a Helm chart with Flux):
apiVersion: helm.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v2
kind: HelmRelease
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  interval: 10m
  chart:
    spec:
      chart: ./charts/order-service
      sourceRef:
        kind: GitRepository
        name: infra-repo
  values:
    replicaCount: 3
    image:
      repository: myregistry/order-service
      tag: 'abc123'  # updated by image-automation-controller

---
# Image automation: auto-update image tag in Git when new image pushed:
apiVersion: image.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1beta2
kind: ImageUpdateAutomation
metadata:
  name: flux-system
spec:
  interval: 1m
  sourceRef: { kind: GitRepository, name: infra-repo }
  git:
    push: { branch: main }
    commit: { messageTemplate: 'ci: update {{range .Updated.Images}}{{println .}}{{end}}' }
  update:
    strategy: Setters  # update image tags in YAML where marked with comments
```

Avoid Flux if you need complex multi-cluster management with a central dashboard (Argo CD's ApplicationSets and multi-cluster UI are more mature).

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: A Kubernetes Operator is a pattern for extending Kubernetes with application-specific operational knowledge — automating complex stateful application management that Kubernetes alone can't handle. An Operator: (1) defines Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs) — new Kubernetes resource types (e.g., `PostgresCluster`, `KafkaTopic`, `ElasticsearchIndex`), (2) runs a controller that watches those CRDs and reconciles desired state → actual state. The Operator encodes the operations knowledge a human DBA/admin would normally perform: 'when I create a PostgresCluster resource, provision a primary + 2 replicas, configure streaming replication, set up backup schedule, and monitor for failover'.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.why_it_exists: Kubernetes manages stateless workloads (Deployments, StatefulSets) well. But databases, message brokers, and complex middleware are stateful and require operational knowledge beyond 'scale up/down': PostgreSQL failover requires promoting a replica to primary. Elasticsearch rolling restarts require pausing shard reallocation. Kafka topic creation requires managing partition assignments. Operators codify this knowledge — replace 'call the DBA' with 'apply a YAML resource'.

# Install the operator CRDs and controller (once):
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cloudnative-pg/cloudnative-pg/main/releases/cnpg-1.24.0.yaml

# Create a PostgreSQL cluster by applying a CRD:
apiVersion: postgresql.cnpg.io/v1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: prod-postgres
spec:
  instances: 3  # 1 primary + 2 replicas
  postgresql:
    parameters:
      max_connections: '200'
      shared_buffers: '512MB'
  storage:
    size: 100Gi
    storageClass: fast-ssd
  backup:
    retentionPolicy: '30d'
    barmanObjectStore:
      destinationPath: s3://my-backups/postgres
      s3Credentials:
        accessKeyId: { name: aws-creds, key: ACCESS_KEY_ID }

# The operator:
# - Creates 3 pods (1 primary, 2 replicas)
# - Configures streaming replication between them
# - Creates a Service (primary) and Service (read-only replicas)

# - Manages rolling updates for PostgreSQL version upgrades

// Writing a simple operator (using controller-runtime):
type DatabaseReconciler struct {
    client.Client
}

func (r *DatabaseReconciler) Reconcile(ctx context.Context, req ctrl.Request) (ctrl.Result, error) {
    // Load the custom resource
    var db myv1.Database
    if err := r.Get(ctx, req.NamespacedName, &db); err != nil {
        return ctrl.Result{}, client.IgnoreNotFound(err)
    }
    // Reconcile: ensure a PostgreSQL pod matches db.Spec
    // Create/update/delete pods and services as needed
    return ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: 5 * time.Minute}, nil
}
```

Use Operator SDK or Kubebuilder to build custom operators for your own applications.

Avoid building a custom operator when an existing one covers your use case (OperatorHub.io has 300+ operators). 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_goes_wrong:
- Operator runaway reconciliation: a reconciler that detects drift, corrects it, triggers an update event, detects drift again, corrects it... in an infinite loop. Fix: use `ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: 5m}` not `{Requeue: true}`, and only requeue after actual status changes, not on every reconcile.
- Finalizer deadlock: an operator adds a finalizer to a resource to perform cleanup on deletion. If the operator is deleted/crashed before running the finalizer, the resource is stuck in `Terminating` state forever. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes — it templates, packages, and deploys collections of Kubernetes resources. Helm: one chart, environment-specific `values.yaml` files. `helm upgrade --install myapp ./chart -f values-production.yaml` applies the templated manifests with production values. These charts are installed millions of times per month. `helm install my-pg bitnami/postgresql --set auth.password=secret` provisions a production-ready PostgreSQL with persistent storage, health checks, HPA, and backup configuration in Kubernetes. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: Kustomize is a Kubernetes configuration customization tool that allows managing multiple environment variants of Kubernetes YAML through overlay patching — no templating language. Structure: a **base** directory (common Kubernetes manifests), **overlays** (per-environment patches that are merged onto the base). Patches can add/replace/delete fields in the base manifests. Built into `kubectl` (`kubectl apply -k ./overlay/production`) and `Argo CD` / `Flux` natively. Key operations: patches (`patchesStrategicMerge`, `patchesJSON6902`), generators (ConfigMap/Secret from files or literals), images (update image tags without editing YAML).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.why_it_exists: Helm's Go template syntax is powerful but complex and error-prone. Kustomize takes a different approach: start with valid Kubernetes YAML (no template syntax), then apply patches. This means: base YAML is deployable as-is (can `kubectl apply -f ./base`), patches are minimal diffs (only what changes), and there's no template rendering step (what you write is what gets applied). Kustomize is simpler for Kubernetes-native teams and works well alongside Helm (you can `helmCharts:` in a Kustomization to include Helm charts as a dependency).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.how_it_works:
```
Directory structure:
base/
  kustomization.yaml
  deployment.yaml
  service.yaml

overlays/
  staging/
    kustomization.yaml
    replica-patch.yaml
  production/
    kustomization.yaml
    replica-patch.yaml
    resource-patch.yaml
```

```yaml
# base/deployment.yaml (valid Kubernetes YAML, no templates)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: order-service
        image: myregistry/order-service:latest
        resources:
          requests: { cpu: 100m, memory: 128Mi }

---
# base/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - deployment.yaml
  - service.yaml

---
# overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
bases:
  - ../../base

images:
  - name: myregistry/order-service
    newTag: 'v1.2.3'  # override image tag without editing base

patchesStrategicMerge:
  - replica-patch.yaml
  - resource-patch.yaml

configMapGenerator:
  - name: app-config
    literals:
      - ENV=production
      - LOG_LEVEL=info

---
# overlays/production/replica-patch.yaml (strategic merge patch)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 5  # override base's replicas: 1

---
# Apply:
kubectl apply -k overlays/production/
# Or with Kustomize CLI:
kustomize build overlays/production/ | kubectl apply -f -
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.use_when: Use Kustomize for: simple multi-environment Kubernetes config management without templating complexity, layering environment-specific patches onto a shared base, and as a complement to Helm (overlay Helm chart output with environment patches). Well-suited for GitOps with Argo CD or Flux (both have native Kustomize support).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.avoid_when: Avoid Kustomize for: distributing reusable application packages (use Helm for packaging — Kustomize has no chart repository concept), complex configuration logic (conditionals, loops — use Helm templating), and when your team is already proficient with Helm and the chart structure is already established.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_goes_wrong:
- Strategic merge patch precedence: a strategic merge patch on a list (e.g., `containers:`) replaces the entire list unless the patch uses the list merge key (`name:`). Forgetting the `name:` key in a container patch results in replacing all containers with just the patched one. Test with `kustomize build` before applying.
- Base/overlay coupling: overlays that reference specific container indexes (`patchesJSON6902` with `/spec/template/spec/containers/0/resources`) break if the base adds a new container before the patched one. Use strategic merge patches with named selectors instead of positional JSON patches.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.real_example: Kubernetes' own deployment uses Kustomize: the official Kubernetes manifests in `kubernetes/kubernetes` repository use Kustomize for cluster component variants. More practically: a team with dev/staging/production clusters: base has 1 replica, 100m CPU; production overlay has 5 replicas, 500m CPU, and production-specific ConfigMap values. The same base YAML is applied to all environments — production overlay patches only what differs. `argocd app create order-service --path overlays/production` — Argo CD renders the Kustomize overlay and applies it automatically.

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: Skaffold is a Google-developed command-line tool that enables continuous local development against Kubernetes — it automates the inner development loop (file change → build image → push → deploy to local cluster). When `skaffold dev` is running: detect file changes → rebuild affected Docker layers → push to local registry → `kubectl apply` updated manifests → port-forward → stream logs. Supports: Docker, Jib (Java), Buildpacks, Ko (Go) for building; Helm, Kustomize, raw manifests for deployment. Key feature: image tagging based on git digest, ensuring each build has a unique tag without manual versioning.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.why_it_exists: Kubernetes local development is painful: change a line of Python → `docker build` (2 min) → `docker push` → `kubectl set image` → wait for pod restart → test → repeat. For a microservices app with 5 services, this is 10 minutes per feedback cycle. Skaffold reduces this to <30 seconds via: layer caching (only rebuild changed layers), direct file sync (skip image rebuild for interpreted languages — sync changed Python files directly into running container), and automatic tag management.

kind: Config
metadata:

build:
  artifacts:
  - image: myregistry/order-service
    context: ./services/order-service
    docker:
      dockerfile: Dockerfile
    sync:
      infer:  # sync changed files directly without rebuild (for dev)
        - '**/*.py'
        - 'static/**'
  - image: myregistry/payment-service
    context: ./services/payment-service

    push: false  # don't push to remote registry in dev mode
    useBuildkit: true

deploy:

    releases:
    - name: myapp

profiles:
- name: production

      releases:
      - name: myapp
        valuesFiles:
        - values-production.yaml
```

```bash

# Ctrl+C: tears down all deployed resources

# One-time build and deploy
skaffold run

# CI pipeline build with git-based tagging
skaffold build --file-output=artifacts.json  # outputs build artifacts with SHA tags
skaffold deploy -a artifacts.json             # deploys the built artifacts

# Run specific profile:

```

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|Mod.what_it_is: Tilt is a local Kubernetes development tool similar to Skaffold but with a more powerful extension model (Tiltfile in Starlark/Python-like syntax) and a superior live UI (web-based dashboard showing all services, logs, and status in real-time). 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.what_it_is: The Richardson Maturity Model (RMM) defines four levels of REST maturity. **Level 0 (Swamp of POX)**: one endpoint, all operations via POST (`POST /api/doThings` with action type in body — essentially RPC). **Level 1 (Resources)**: separate endpoints per resource (`/orders`, `/users`) but only `POST`. **Level 2 (HTTP Verbs)**: proper use of `GET`, `POST`, `PUT`, `DELETE`, `PATCH` with correct HTTP status codes. **Level 3 (Hypermedia/HATEOAS)**: responses include links to related actions (`_links` with `pay`, `cancel` URLs). Most real-world 'REST' APIs are Level 2; true Level 3 (HATEOAS) is rare.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.why_it_exists: Many APIs claim to be RESTful while violating REST constraints. The RMM provides a structured way to assess API maturity and identify improvement areas. SOAP/WSDL APIs are typically Level 0. Well-designed REST APIs target Level 2. Hypermedia-driven APIs (some banking APIs, Paypal's API) target Level 3. Understanding the maturity level helps teams know what 'REST' actually means and evaluate trade-offs.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.how_it_works:
```
Level 0 → Level 3 progression:

Level 0 (Swamp of POX — Plain Old XML/JSON):
  POST /api
  Body: {"action": "getOrder", "orderId": 123}
  Response: 200 + any response (always 200, even on errors)
  This is essentially SOAP/XML-RPC over HTTP

Level 1 (Resources):
  POST /api/orders
  POST /api/orders/123  (body: {"action": "getOrder"})
  Resources have URLs but HTTP verbs are ignored

Level 2 (HTTP Verbs + Status Codes) — most real-world APIs:
  GET    /api/orders         200 + array
  GET    /api/orders/123     200 + object (or 404)
  POST   /api/orders         201 + Location header
  PUT    /api/orders/123     200 (replace) or 404
  PATCH  /api/orders/123     200 (partial update)
  DELETE /api/orders/123     204 (no content)

Level 3 (HATEOAS — Hypermedia as Engine of Application State):
  GET /api/orders/123
  → {
    "id": 123,
    "status": "pending",
    "total": 99.99,
    "_links": {
      "self": { "href": "/api/orders/123" },
      "pay":  { "href": "/api/orders/123/payment", "method": "POST" },
      "cancel": { "href": "/api/orders/123/cancel", "method": "DELETE" }
    }
  }
  Clients don't hardcode URLs — they follow links from responses
  Spring HATEOAS, Siren, HAL are Level 3 implementations
```
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.use_when: Target Level 2 for all new REST APIs — it's the practical optimum. Level 3 is valuable for APIs that support many different clients where URL discovery and API evolution without client changes are important. Use RMM during API design reviews to assess and communicate the intended API style.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.avoid_when: Don't treat Level 3 as always better than Level 2. HATEOAS adds complexity (link generation, client link-following) that many teams don't need. A Level 2 API with good documentation is often better than a Level 3 API with underdocumented link semantics.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.what_goes_wrong: - Level 2 with Level 0 error handling: API returns `200 OK { 'error': 'order not found' }` — mixing Level 2 resource design with Level 0 error handling. Always use HTTP status codes for errors: `404 Not Found` for missing resources, `422` for validation errors. This is the most common Level 2 API mistake.
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.real_example: Paypal's REST API (v1): a Level 3 implementation. `POST /v1/payments/payment` returns a payment with links: `[{rel: 'approval_url', href: 'https://...paypal.com/checkoutnow?token=...', method: 'REDIRECT'}]`. The client follows the `approval_url` link — it doesn't construct this URL itself. When Paypal changes the approval URL structure, clients that follow links adapt automatically without code changes. GitHub's v3 REST API is Level 2; GitHub's v4 API is GraphQL (bypassing the REST maturity model entirely).

15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.what_it_is: API-first development treats the API contract as the primary artifact — designed and agreed upon before any implementation begins. Process: (1) define the API in OpenAPI/AsyncAPI spec, (2) stakeholders review and approve the contract, (3) backend generates server stubs from the spec, (4) frontend generates client code from the spec, (5) backend and frontend develop in parallel against the spec (using mock servers). The spec is the contract, the truth — implementation follows the spec, not the other way around ('code-first' generates the spec from existing code, often after the fact).
15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.why_it_exists: Traditional 'code-first' API development: backend implements endpoints, frontend integrates, discovers missing fields or wrong types, backend changes the API, frontend breaks, cycle repeats. 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.what_it_is: JSON:API (not just 'JSON') is a specification (`jsonapi.org`) for building APIs that use JSON — prescribing exact response and request envelope format. A JSON:API response has: `data` (primary resource — type, id, attributes, relationships, links), `included` (related resources, eliminating over-fetching), `errors` (structured error array), `meta` (non-standard metadata), `links` (pagination). 15|🔴 T1 🔬 New & Deep Research Topics|API.avoid_when: Avoid JSON:API for: simple APIs where the envelope verbosity (`data.type`, `data.attributes`, `data.relationships`) adds more complexity than value, REST APIs that will be publicly documented and consumed by developers unfamiliar with JSON:API (learning curve), and when existing team conventions are already well-established and consistent.
